papers.title: Arithmetic Universality and Integer Decomposition in Disjunctions of Three Staircase Simplices
TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases
papers.abstract: Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks. We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference. We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.

papers.title: Toeplitz coefficients and the Lu-Tian correspondence on Sasakian manifolds
No Supersoft X-rays Before SN 2026ahvu: Constraints on a Potentially Prompt Type Ia Progenitor
papers.abstract: The nearby Type Ia supernova SN 2026ahvu offers a rare opportunity to probe its progenitor that may have evolved unusually rapidly. If the progenitor formed in either of the two young stellar clusters near the explosion site in NGC 1433, the delay from star formation to explosion could have been $\sim$100 Myr or less. The distance to NGC 1433 remains uncertain, with published estimates of 9.1 Mpc and 18.9 Mpc. Our preliminary fit to the rising ATLAS light curve yields a distance of $17.7^{+1.5}_{-1.4}$ Mpc. In the classical single-degenerate scenario, a white dwarf steadily burning hydrogen accreted from a non-degenerate companion can emit detectable supersoft X-rays before explosion. We search for this emission using two archival Chandra observations obtained before the explosion. The observations provide a combined exposure of 95.3 ks, with no 0.3-7 keV photons detected within 2" of the supernova position. For a 100 eV blackbody with Galactic foreground absorption, the 95\% bolometric luminosity limits are $6.3\times10^{37}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and $2.7\times10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ at 9.1 Mpc and 18.9 Mpc, respectively. At both distances, the observations exclude a hot, compact white dwarf undergoing steady hydrogen burning if the absorption is limited to the Galactic foreground. However, cooler, expanded, or more heavily absorbed photospheres remain viable. Together with the pre-explosion non-detections for SN 2011fe and SN 2014J, our results reinforce the absence of luminous supersoft progenitors in nearby SNe Ia. This pattern is naturally consistent with double-degenerate explosions, although X-ray-faint single-degenerate configurations remain viable. Post-explosion X-ray observations can test for circumstellar interaction and help determine whether material around the progenitor could have obscured a luminous nuclear burning white dwarf.

papers.title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
papers.abstract: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.

papers.title: Fourier--Stieltjes palettes on compact abelian groups
MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

papers.title: Generating a simple silicon detector simulation with an open-weight large language model
papers.abstract: Recent LLM developments have seen AI-generated code become commonplace in the software development industry. Without tool access, LLMs cannot execute simulations, and their knowledge of toolkits such as Geant4 is limited. We demonstrate here, a detector simulation workflow with a Qwen3.6-27B model with Q4_K_M GGUF quantisation together with custom resources and tools served via MCP servers to generate a particle detector simulation. In 50 independent runs, 42(29--56)% at 95% CI produced energy-deposit distributions statistically consistent with a reference simulation, measured against a reference simulation. These results provide a proof of concept that MC simulations can be generated using text-based prompts with an LLM, given the necessary resources and tools. More extensive resources, such as example code and additional documentation, are likely to be required for more complex simulation tasks.

papers.title: On the origin of Milky Way binary black holes with LISA
papers.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may constitute a fraction of dark matter, but distinguishing them from black holes of stellar origin remains a major challenge. We propose a new method based on the three-dimensional localization of Galactic Binary Black Holes (BBHs) by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). While stellar-origin BBHs are expected to be associated with the stellar distribution of the Milky Way, PBHs may trace its more extended dark matter halo. We introduce a spatial overlap ratio that compares the gravitational-wave localization of each binary with the normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. Using a Fisher-matrix forecast and 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission, we find that detecting three BBHs with an overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in approximately 99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in fewer than 0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even when including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass. These results suggest that the localization of only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, offering an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.

papers.title: Why Cassini's Oval Could Not Replace Kepler's Ellipse?
papers.abstract: In the later seventeenth century, Kepler's ellipse was not yet accepted. Ward claimed that Boulliau's conic hypothesis amounted to a Ptolemaic equant at the ellipse's empty focus, and built his own model on it. Around 1675--1680, Giovanni Domenico Cassini proposed another curve, the ``oval'', a genus-1 quartic with no closed-form Kepler equation; yet its eccentric anomaly shares exactly the leading coefficient of Kepler's, and its empty focus is, for the Sun, 38 times closer to a true equant than the ellipse's. Dynamically, Binet's formula shows that the force producing the oval under the area law departs from the inverse square by an index $\mathcal{D}(e)\sim3/(4e^2)$, depending on the oval's parameter $e$: no single exponent serves the whole family. This absence of universality, not of an area law, distinguishes it from the ellipse, and arguably explains why Cassini, the Académie and Leibniz kept the question open after the \emph{Principia} (1687).

papers.title: Anchoring Motion, Refining Trajectories: Generalizable Continuous Neural Decoding
papers.abstract: Brain activity encodes motor information across multiple temporal scales, enabling continuous neural control beyond discrete action recognition. However, existing methods are typically tailored to specific subjects and tasks, with direct neural-to-kinematic mappings that can entangle subject-specific neural variability with task-dependent motion patterns, limiting generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce AMRT, a shared neural decoding framework for heterogeneous electrode configurations and movement paradigms. Motivated by cortical encoding of movement direction and speed, AMRT adopts a two-stage design that anchors local motion through velocity estimation and refines the resulting trajectories over longer horizons, encouraging reuse of local motion tendencies across subjects and tasks. Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

papers.title: Real-world Polarimetric Environment Map Dataset
papers.abstract: Environment maps are a standard representation of illumination, enabling realistic image-based lighting in modern rendering systems. However, existing environment maps typically encode only RGB radiance, omitting polarization, an intrinsic property of light that is imperceptible to the human eye but informative about surface shape and material properties. This omission precludes the physically accurate simulation of polarized light transport under in-the-wild illumination conditions, heavily limiting the development and evaluation of robust polarization-based scene reconstruction and understanding methods. We address this gap by introducing a real-world polarimetric environment map dataset, each providing a full-sphere panorama with per-pixel high-dynamic-range RGB Stokes vectors. To acquire the dataset, we design and calibrate a dedicated imaging system and develop a polarization-aware panorama-stitching pipeline. In particular, we introduce a frame-field representation for perspective cameras, together with singularity-aware blending, to enable smooth polarimetric panorama stitching without singularity artifacts. Using this system, we capture 100 polarimetric environment maps across diverse real-world scenes. We further develop a custom rendering plugin and demonstrate close agreement between real and rendered observations. Finally, we analyze the polarization state of the sky across different times and weather conditions, and demonstrate its practical impact on a downstream shape-from-polarization task.

papers.title: Non-factorisable Yangian Lax matrices through oscillators
papers.abstract: We construct oscillator realisations of Yangian Lax operators in type $A$, with particular interest in non-factorisable operators associated with prime snake modules. Our construction applies to finite-dimensional skew representations of $Y(\mathfrak{gl}_n)$. We prove that these representations are generated by the tensor vacuum in suitably ordered tensor products of oscillator representations. Their Lax operators are obtained by restricting the corresponding products of linear oscillator Lax operators to these submodules. We determine the vacuum eigenvalues and Drinfeld polynomials, and give a determinant formula for the dimensions directly in terms of the highest loop weights. A $21$-dimensional example illustrates the construction, including an explicit basis and a transfer-matrix identity.

papers.title: Experimentally relevant witness for non-Markovianity in discrete time crystals
papers.abstract: Discrete time crystals (DTCs) are almost always analyzed under the Born-Markov approximation, in which the environment is memoryless. We show that a reservoir with a finite correlation time $\tau_m$ leaves an exact and strikingly simple imprint on the stroboscopic dynamics of DTCs, which can be used as an experimentally relevant witness for non-Markovianity. By analyzing a post-Markovian master equation we prove that the Floquet spectrum splits into the ordinary Markovian spectrum plus a replica of the purely unitary Floquet spectrum, uniformly contracted by $e^{-T/\tau_m}$, where $T$ is the drive period. Consequently, the DTC signal decay rate becomes independent of any system parameter once $\tau_m$ exceeds the Markovian lifetime of the DTC. The measured decay, and in particular its insensitivity to tunable system parameters, thus becomes a direct read-out of the reservoir correlation time. Below this threshold the dynamics is already non-Markovian, but the memory remains hidden in the decay. We confirm this in two structurally unrelated DTCs, a collective long-range model with incoherent pumping and a disorder-free Ising chain with dephasing, where a single estimator recovers $\tau_m$. The time crystal thereby witnesses the non-Markovianity of its own environment.

papers.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

papers.title: An Alternative to Crawlers: Scalable P2P Network Monitoring Using the Network Scale-Up Method
papers.abstract: \Ac{p2p} networks have remained an active area of research and development for decades. Originally used for data dissemination, they have later become instrumental to decentralized payment systems, blockchains, and Web3 applications. Since decentralization is a crucial property of these networks, they are continuously monitored to track attributes such as the geographical distribution of nodes, which serve as indicators of infrastructure concentration and resilience. However, monitoring typically relies on network crawls to derive accurate snapshots, which requires substantial computational and network resources. In contrast, \ac{nsum} is a statistical tool that estimates the prevalence of subpopulations based on responses to questions such as \enquote{How many people do you know in a specific group?} This work leverages the information embedded in Kademlia routing tables to develop a lightweight \ac{nsum}-based measurement and estimation framework that infers global network attribute distributions from a small set of nodes, offering an alternative to full-network crawls. As a case study, we evaluate our approach on \ac{ipfs}, a well-researched and widely used Web3 data storage and retrieval network. This is the first application of \ac{nsum} to decentralized network measurement. We evaluate our methodology on two datasets: the first comprises 360 full-network crawls collected over one month to assess our measurement-estimation approach across multiple simulated measurement scenarios, while the second dataset was collected through a deployment of the proposed lightweight measurement framework during May 2026. The results show that local Kademlia routing views, with only 10 nodes, preserve sufficient information to accurately estimate global attribute distributions, achieving normalized biases below \SI{10}{\percent} and closely tracking temporal changes in network composition.

papers.title: Convex polynomial approximation on the unit ball
A description of the space with no separable quotient presented by OpenAI
tsspiral: An R Package to Create Circular Versions of Time Series Plots
papers.abstract: `tsspiral` is an open-source R package that introduces a circular approach to time series visualisation using polar coordinates. We refer to this circular representation of time series data as a spiral. `tsspiral` provides a collection of `ggplot2` geometries for creating a spiral representation of time series data. In our approach, we arrange observations around a circle. Each year is represented by a circle, with the angular position corresponding to the day of the year, and successive years appear as concentric rings. This arrangement facilitates the exploration of periodicity, seasonality, and recurring temporal patterns, particularly in long time series. The package also supports temporal hierarchical visualisations to compare patterns across time scales. By bringing polar-coordinate-based visualisation into routine time series analysis, `tsspiral` offers a practical tool for exploring temporal patterns and communicating complex time-dependent structures. Rather than treating spiral plots as standalone graphics, our approach brings them into the grammar of graphics framework, enabling users to explore temporal patterns through a broader range of visual encodings.

papers.title: Neural Marked Point Processes for Health Insurance Claims
papers.abstract: Health insurance claims exhibit temporal dependence, as previous claims may provide information about the timing, type and amount of subsequent claims. Such dependencies are difficult to capture with traditional actuarial models based on aggregated claim counts. We investigate a neural marked point process in which a causal Transformer represents individual claim histories and determines type-specific conditional intensities, allowing for self-excitation and interactions between claim types. The framework also incorporates conditional severity distributions, reporting delays and stochastic medical-cost inflation. We develop a likelihood-based calibration procedure that accounts for incomplete claim reporting and evaluate the model using both simulated and empirical data. A simulation study with 10,000 insurance contracts examines the recovery of known claim dynamics, while an application to MEPS-derived medical-event data assesses predictive performance. The fitted model reproduces the main patterns in claim frequencies and severities, although some discrepancies remain in the tails of the distributions. On the MEPS data, the neural model achieves better predictive performance than two generalized linear model benchmarks in terms of claim-count deviance and expenditure discrimination.

papers.title: A scaling approach to double phase equations in $\mathbb{R}^N$
The pinched Veronese has no Koszul filtration
Detectability of Eccentric Intermediate Mass-Ratio Inspiral in the Decihertz Band
papers.abstract: The proposed decihertz gravitational-wave (GW) band $(\sim 10^{-2}-1\,\Hz)$ will observe the late inspiral of intermediate mass-ratio inspirals (IMRIs), binaries with mass ratios $10^2 \lesssim q \lesssim 10^4$ that assemble dynamically in dense stellar environments and are expected to retain measurable eccentricity. Search and parameter-estimation pipelines are predominantly built around circular templates, and we test this assumption. Using black-hole perturbation theory waveforms from \textsc{FastEMRIWaveforms} for a representative IMRI ($M=10^4\,\modot$, $q=100$, observed for its final $10\,\hr$), we compute fitting factors between eccentric signals and circular templates, maximizing over the template's total mass and mass ratio with a differential-evolution search, for the B-DECIGO, LGWA-Si, and IndIGO-D noise curves and a flat PSD. The mismatch grows with initial eccentricity $e_0$ and crosses the standard $3\%$ threshold at $e_0\simeq3\times10^{-2}$, well within the range allowed by the waveform model and expected from dynamical formation. The best-fitting circular templates also bias the total mass and mass ratio by several percent at $e_0=0.1$. Combining the mismatch with the signal-to-noise-dependent distinguishability criterion, we find that for a source at $1\,\mathrm{Gpc}$, eccentricities as small as $e_0\simeq5\times10^{-4}$ (B-DECIGO and IndIGO-D) and $5\times10^{-3}$ (LGWA-Si) are resolvable, one to two orders of magnitude below where detection efficiency degrades. The loss of match arises from the excitation of radial Teukolsky harmonics, which spread power into sidebands that circular templates cannot represent, and from the slower orbital decay of eccentric binaries at fixed initial semi-latus rectum. Robust detection and parameter estimation of IMRIs with DECIGO, LGWA, and IndIGO-D will require eccentric waveform models and template banks.

papers.title: RevealLO: Global-Scale FWI Including Long-Period Major-Arc Surface Wave and Multi-Orbit Body Wave Data
papers.abstract: Global full-waveform inversion (FWI) has matured significantly in recent years, but resolution in the southern hemisphere often remains limited due to sparse receiver coverage. To address this problem, we constructed RevealLO, a global-scale FWI model that updates its predecessor REVEAL by expanding the inversion time window from 1 hour to 3.5 hours. The extended time window incorporates both minor-arc ($R_1, G_1$) and major-arc ($R_2, G_2$) surface wave arrivals, as well as late-arriving multi-orbit body waves, thereby increasing azimuthal coverage beneath ocean basins and the southern hemisphere. We simulate 3-D viscoelastic wavefields using the spectral-element solver Salvus on global fourth-order cubed-sphere meshes, and update velocity structure by successively broadening the period band from 100 - 200 s to 60 - 200 s. Measurements and adjoint sources are based on time-frequency phase misfits, which are suitable for both large-amplitude surface and low-amplitude multiply-reflected body waves. For iterative optimization, we employ a mini-batch stochastic trust-region L-BFGS algorithm, followed by mesh reprojection onto the $33~s$ REVEAL baseline mesh and lowermost-mantle regularization. RevealLO preserves short-period whole-Earth body wave fits while improving azimuthal sampling and mitigating trade-offs between unmodeled azimuthal anisotropy and isotropic structure in the upper and mid mantle.

papers.title: TCBP-JOBS: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Error Correction Decoding and Noise Learning with Near-Optimal Accuracy
Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
papers.abstract: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

papers.title: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is a natural alternative because it decomposes a signal across scales. A growing body of work makes the wavelet filter learnable, on the assumption that a more flexible wavelet forecasts better. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. We introduce a forecaster that turns a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows that share a dominant scale. Three findings follow. First, most of the improvement is there before any filter is learned. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. In practice, start from any valid wavelet, cache the patch boundaries once and treat training the filter as a per-dataset decision rather than a default.

papers.title: Narrowband active noise control for continuous wave operation of TESLA cavities
papers.abstract: TESLA 9-cell elliptical cavities are used in the accelerators of the European XFEL and LCLS-II. The high duty cycle upgrade study for EuXFEL and the LCLS-II-HE program target loaded quality factors of 6.10^7 and beyond, leading to RF cavity half bandwidths below 11 Hz. Stable operation in these conditions heavily relies on active RF resonance control, since the RF drive power required to maintain amplitude and phase lock would surpass amplifier max ratings if detuning is not compensated. To counteract mechanical vibrations, e.g. introduced by rotational machines in the proximity of the accelerating modules, a dedicated narrowband active noise control algorithm was introduced in previous work. This proceeding presents CPU based implementations and latest test results obtained at the Cryomodule Test Bench (CMTB) at DESY and LCLS-II at SLAC, where the stable operation gradient of a cavity could be increased from 9 to 15 MV/m without violating RF control limits.

papers.title: Non-thermal emission from molecular clouds illuminated by continuous cosmic-ray accelerators: application to the stellar cluster W43
papers.abstract: Context: Cosmic rays escaping from their accelerators produce gamma-ray emission through interactions with ambient gas. While the scenario of an impulsive injection of cosmic rays has been extensively studied, that of a continuous injection in time has received comparatively less attention. The latter scenario is particularly relevant for stellar clusters, which may contribute to a non-negligible fraction of Galactic cosmic rays. Aims: We intend to characterize the excesses of cosmic rays around their accelerators and to assess the detectability of the gamma-ray emission resulting from the interactions of cosmic rays in nearby molecular clouds. We focus in particular on star clusters and seek to apply these considerations to the case of W43. Methods: We derive analytical estimates for the cosmic ray excess around sources as a function of source properties and transport parameters. We also evaluate under which conditions the predicted gamma-ray emission from illuminated molecular clouds can be detected by current and future instruments. We then apply these results to explain the gamma-ray emission from the the W43 region. Results: We find that producing detectable gamma-ray emission from molecular clouds illuminated by cosmic rays escaping from star clusters generally requires either suppressed diffusion relative to the Galactic value or anisotropic diffusion, with the latter scenario requiring a smaller global energetic. We applied this approach to the case of W43 and by fitting its gamma-ray emission we were able to constrain the underlying CR transport parameters.

papers.title: Continuous Kakeya type problems with special points that sweep much more area than the rest
Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
papers.abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

papers.title: Reference Replay for Excitation Injection and Subsequent Exponential Convergence under Concurrent Learning Adaptive Control
papers.abstract: Concurrent learning (CL) guarantees precise identification of unknown parameters---if data with finite excitation (FE) happens to be collected online. To improve the reliability of CL, this work establishes a mechanism allowing FE-occurrence to be verified a priori: We propose replaying a given training segment in the reference until data with finite excitation is collected online. Provided the training segment fulfills a certain off-line excitation test, FE then occurs in unknown, but finite time. Moreover, we provide an upper bound on the time-to-FE. Even though this bound involves a dependency on the unknown initial Lyapunov-function value, its structure shows that FE occurs in arbitrarily early replay cycles when increasing the control gain; which may motivate employing a high-gain strategy. The theoretical findings are verified on an academic simulation example.

papers.title: Robust Optimal Network Reduction for Distribution Systems
papers.abstract: Network reduction replaces large networks with smaller equivalents to speed up power flow and optimization studies. Optimal Kron-based Reduction of Networks (Opti-KRON) finds the optimal set of nodes to faithfully represent a large-scale radial network for representative loading scenarios. Under unseen nodal injections, however, its accuracy can drop. This paper extends Opti-KRON to uncertain nodal injections using robust uncertainty sets and a Wasserstein ambiguity set, with voltage magnitude error guarantees. To improve scalability, we develop a presolve screening step to eliminate redundant constraints and variables while preserving the feasible set. We also adopt adversarial constraint generation to reduce memory requirements by iteratively adding worst-case nodal injections. On a real 8,387-node feeder at a threshold of 0.001~p.u., the reduction removes 49.9% of the nodes. For one uncertainty set, adversarial constraint generation cuts the required memory by a factor of more than 18.

papers.title: PointZip: Statistically Lossless Compression for Climate Data with Pointwise Error Bounds
papers.abstract: High-resolution climate simulations generate data volumes that increasingly strain storage, I/O, and data dissemination. Error-bounded lossy compressors can reduce these costs, but their tolerances are usually user-chosen and difficult to standardize across heterogeneous climate datasets. We address this limitation with statistically lossless compression, where the pointwise compression error is bounded by the pointwise data uncertainty. We propose PointZip, a two-stage compressor that combines a rate-distortion-efficient base layer with error-bound-aware residual coding to enforce pointwise guarantees. On outputs from the widely used climate modeling framework ICON, PointZip makes 1km simulations practical by reducing storage bandwidth requirements by 72x. On the ERA5 climate dataset, PointZip reaches 69.3x on the most representative variables, reducing the commonly used subset to 4 TB. In downstream evaluations, PointZip preserves data spectra, extreme events, and air parcel trajectories, while increasing neural weather forecast RMSE by less than 1%, with negligible impact on the Fractions Skill Score (FSS).

papers.title: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in low-altitude airspace increases the risk of unauthorized intrusions, making reliable detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs essential for low-altitude airspace safety. However, the existing public UAV datasets are mostly acquired from fixed ground-based viewpoints and are limited to imaging or radio-frequency (RF) observations, which restricts the sensing coverage and deployment flexibility. To address this gap, we present A2A-UAV, a multimodal air-to-air dataset for UAV detection and identification. Specifically, 15 target UAVs of 13 commercial models were recorded at three outdoor sites under daytime and nighttime conditions by using a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar. The dataset contains 105,294 time-aligned samples of RGB, panoramic, thermal, and RF time-frequency images and radar point clouds. Moreover, all 209,539 bounding boxes of the predominantly small UAV targets were manually annotated and cross-checked. Therefore, A2A-UAV provides a valuable resource for air-to-air UAV detection, identification, and multimodal fusion in low-altitude airspace.

papers.title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
papers.abstract: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

papers.title: Safe Physical Interaction of All-Electric Heavy-Duty Robotic Manipulators via Control Barrier Functions and Variable Impedance Control
papers.abstract: All-electric heavy-duty robotic manipulators are increasingly expected to operate close to tunnel walls, equipment, and other structures while retaining the force capability required for large-payload tasks. Accurate motion control alone does not address the resulting safety and interaction requirements. This paper develops a safety-aware physical-interaction architecture that combines variable impedance control (VIC) with control barrier functions (CBFs) on top of an established virtual decomposition control (VDC) framework for electromechanical linear actuator (EMLA)-driven manipulators. VIC continuously adapts the task-space stiffness and damping according to predicted proximity and contact risk, whereas a joint-velocity CBF filter enforces Cartesian workspace boundaries and the physical stroke limits induced by the closed-chain lift and tilt mechanisms. To account for nonideal realization of the filtered velocity by the inner VDC/EMLA dynamics, the CBF inequalities are tightened using a measured bound on the joint-velocity tracking error. Four configurations, namely VDC, VIC+VDC, CBF+VDC, and VIC+CBF+VDC, are evaluated under workspace, actuator-limit, and physical-interaction scenarios. VIC reduces the peak and RMS environment-interaction forces by 92.59% and 96.33%, respectively; both robust CBF configurations maintain positive workspace and EMLA safety margins, while VIC+CBF+VDC reduces the CBF intervention metric by 10.30% compared with CBF+VDC.

papers.title: Rotation-Invariant Machine Learning for Highly Symmetric Molecular Configurations
papers.abstract: Atomistic machine learning can approximate expensive quantum mechanical calculations at a fraction of their computational cost, but accuracy depends strongly on how the three-dimensional atomic environments are represented. Invariant representations enable fast computation but can fail to distinguish geometrically distinct configurations, especially in highly symmetric environments. We introduce a lightweight benchmark to evaluate expressivity on $n$-fold symmetric configurations, and use it to expose degeneracies in both invariant and equivariant architectures. Guided by these results, we construct a new invariant basis for HIP-HOP which resolves most of the identified failures. On a methane simulation dataset, the extended basis achieves the lowest error among the HIP-HOP variants and has similar accuracy to EquiformerV3 while running $3.2\times$ faster at inference. These results show that carefully constructed invariant representations can mitigate key expressivity limitations while balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Programmable Semantic Interventions: Learning Causal Carriers from Behavioral Programs
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction explains a frozen network by aligning its activations with the variables of a simpler, interpretable model, and checking that interventions on the two agree. Finding such an alignment currently requires a counterfactual dataset: for every pair of prompts, the answer the network ought to give once the variable has been changed. In practice, those labels are produced by an executable algorithm for the behavior, written before studying the model supposed to implement it. However, the criterion these methods optimize only leverages the answer an intervention should produce. Here, we develop an approach that lets the investigator define that relationship directly: the answers the variable can produce, and which of them an intervention should yield. We call this interface a semantic program and introduce Programmable Semantic Interventions (PSI): a low-rank activation subspace learned so that interchanging it changes the model's answer as the program declares, with the expected answers read from the frozen model itself. On the MIB benchmark PSI performs on par with supervised alignment at matched data and training budget, without curated pairs, and it needs no ground-truth labels; while on natural science questions with gold labels withheld, it tracks the model's own answers better than a subspace trained on gold labels. The declaration also fixes a coordinate system with known semantics, enabling donor-free steering: jointly training PSI for both localization and control realizes 94.8% of held-out requests for answers the investigator chooses, without the need for donor prompts.

papers.title: Share your Screen and Talk to Gemini: How Young Learners Interact with Multimodal GenAI While Solving Scratch Tasks
papers.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.

papers.title: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $\mu(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((\kappa^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

papers.title: Fix, Don't Retake: Physics-Simulated Training for Correcting Patient Positioning Errors in Dental Panoramic Radiographs
papers.abstract: Patient-positioning errors can distort panoramic radiographs and lead to repeat examinations. This study investigated artificial intelligence for correcting these errors in existing images. A physics-based simulator generated paired correctly positioned and mispositioned panoramics from cone-beam computed tomography volumes, with controlled individual and combined positioning errors. Five approaches were compared: U-Net, pix2pix, conditional diffusion, an error-conditioned model, and a mixture of error-specific specialists. Evaluation used image similarity and geometric metrics across three test sets. All approaches improved mean image similarity and reduced geometric errors, with U-Net and the two error-aware approaches outperforming pix2pix and conditional diffusion.

papers.title: Syllable- and Word-Level Evaluation of Tibetan OCR
papers.abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) for Tibetan is evaluated predominantly by character error rate (CER). Tibetan marks syllable boundaries but does not mark word boundaries, so a word error rate requires a segmenter. This study evaluates nine recognizer configurations on typeset, woodblock and two handwritten script styles, alone and in combination, and reports syllable- and word-level error rates, to our knowledge the first for Tibetan OCR. The configurations span CTC models, TrOCR encoder-decoders with and without post-training quantization, and a vision-language model, and each is scored under CER, the syllable error rate (SER) and three segmented word error rates (SWER). CER ranks systems largely as the higher-level rates do (Kendall $\tau \geq 0.833$), with one pair ordered oppositely. On the effect of joint training, CER and SER record significant changes of opposite sign in 7 of 64 comparisons. SER needs no segmenter and ranks systems as SWER does under two of the three segmenters ($\tau \geq 0.889$). The output of each configuration is also tagged for part of speech, annotated for named entities and machine translated, and each result is compared with that obtained on the reference text. As rough guidance, translation chrF of 60 is reached at SER of 0.047 or below and part-of-speech preservation of 0.8 at 0.078 or below, while no error rate separates the systems that reach entity preservation of 0.6 from those that do not.

papers.title: Déjà-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating
papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

papers.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.

papers.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark
papers.abstract: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.

papers.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

papers.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
papers.abstract: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

papers.title: Stability manifolds and resolutions of singularities
Lifting asymptotic symmetries from metric to tetrad formulation
papers.abstract: Metric solution spaces defined by gauge and boundary conditions are associated with a residual symmetry algebra, consisting of the diffeomorphism generators whose action preserves these conditions. Describing a metric solution space in terms of tetrad variables adds a local Lorentz freedom. When part of this freedom is fixed by additional tetrad gauge and boundary conditions, metric residual symmetries must be supplemented by compensating Lorentz transformations. If a residual Lorentz freedom remains, there is an ambiguity in these compensating transformations. The most direct choices generally fail to realize the metric residual symmetry algebra as a subalgebra of the tetrad one, because of a field-dependent cocycle. We show that a reference tetrad, that is a section of the tetrad solution space seen as a principal bundle over the metric one, always provides a lift free of this cocycle, so that the tetrad residual symmetry algebra is the semi-direct sum of the metric one and the ideal of field-dependent residual Lorentz transformations. The construction is independent of the gauge conditions, of the residual group, of the first-order Lagrangian, and reduces to the Kosmann lift on metric isometry generators. We illustrate it on a Weyl BMS-type solution space with time-dependent boundary metric, described in tetrad variables with a residual U(1) Lorentz freedom, for which the cocycle of a naive lift is computed and then explicitly removed.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

papers.title: Constant-Factor Matching-Size Estimation in Random-Order Streams
papers.abstract: We give a one-pass algorithm that estimates the maximum matching size of an arbitrary simple graph within a constant factor using $O(\log^2 n)$ bits of space. The edges arrive exactly once in uniformly random order. The algorithm succeeds with probability at least $2/3$, does not require the number of edges in advance, and has worst-case total running time $O((m+1)\log(n+2))$ on a word RAM. Kapralov, Khanna, and Sudan (SODA 2014) obtained a polylogarithmic approximation in polylogarithmic space. Kapralov, Mitrović, Norouzi-Fard, and Tardos (SODA 2020) subsequently gave a constant-factor approximation from independent uniform edge samples and an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation in random order. We obtain a constant factor in the latter model with the same $O(\log^2 n)$ space bound. The main ingredient is a comparison between the memory states of a recursive sampling algorithm under sampling with and without replacement. We account jointly for the sampled edges retained by the recursion and the positions at which they arrived. Randomized thresholds limit the additional information stored in numerical counters. A bound on the expected work of the entire recursion then removes the loss from its logarithmic depth. The resulting estimator repeatedly improves a coarse estimate while storing only one recursion stack.

papers.title: Radiofrequency disorientation in migratory birds: radical pairs or a separate sensory system?
papers.abstract: Alongside other directional cues, migratory songbirds use the Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate the hundreds or thousands of kilometres between their breeding and over-wintering sites. If it seems surprising that an animal can extract information from a magnetic field a hundred times weaker than a small refrigerator magnet, it should be astounding that this ability can be disrupted by radiofrequency magnetic fields thousands of times weaker still. Magnetic fields with strengths between 1 and 100 nT and frequencies between 0.1 and 100 MHz have been found to prevent captive night-migratory songbirds from orienting in the geomagnetic field (25-65 microtesla, depending on geographic location). Remarkably, the frequency dependence of this disruption agrees closely with predictions for radical pairs in cryptochrome (the leading hypothesis for the mechanism of the avian magnetic compass), whereas the extraordinarily weak fields that cause disorientation are difficult to reconcile with conventional radical-pair theory. This perspective examines the evidence for radiofrequency-induced disorientation and its relationship to the cryptochrome hypothesis. It concludes by considering a suggestion that birds may possess a distinct radiofrequency-sensitive system based on electromagnetic induction.

papers.title: AnachroBench: Evaluating Historical Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
papers.abstract: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at this http URL .

papers.title: FM-Recon: Exploring Foundation Model Features for Accelerated Cardiac Cine MRI Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across various medical imaging tasks, yet their potential for MRI reconstruction remains largely unexplored, particularly within unrolled reconstruction networks and under artifact-corrupted inputs. In this work, we explore whether and how features from pretrained foundation models can benefit accelerated cardiac cine MRI reconstruction. To this end, we propose FM-Recon, a framework that refines and integrates extracted features from frozen image encoder of foundation models into an unrolled reconstruction network. Through extensive experiments on the CMRxRecon2023 dataset, we systematically evaluate foundation model features across different reconstruction settings. Our results show that foundation models can extract informative representations from artifact-corrupted inputs and improve reconstruction performance, particularly at moderate acceleration factors. These findings demonstrate the potential of foundation model features for accelerated MRI reconstruction and provide insights into their effective integration into unrolled reconstruction networks.

papers.title: Generalized transverse-momentum-dependent parton distributions of a photon and orbital angular momentum
papers.abstract: The coefficients of generalized transverse-momentum-dependent distributions (GTMDs) that encode the canonical fermion orbital angular momentum and spin--orbit correlation do not contribute to the direct transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) and generalized-parton-distribution (GPD) projections. We present, to our knowledge, the first explicit calculation of the leading-twist, time-even, chiral-even fermion GTMDs of an on-shell real photon at zero skewness and order $\alpha$. The coefficients $\mathcal{F}_A$ and $\mathcal{G}_A$, which multiply the $k_\perp\times\Delta_\perp$ structure, yield the fermion orbital angular momentum $\ell_z^f$ and spin--orbit correlation $\mathcal{C}_z^f$. For photon helicity $+1$, both are obtained in closed form in the leading fermion--antifermion sector and obey $\mathcal{C}_z^f=-\ell_z^f/2$ for a common transverse regulator independent of $x$, because the channel with the active fermion's spin anti-aligned with its orbital motion carries three times the integrated weight of the aligned channel. The projections reproduce the known photon TMDs and leading-logarithmic photon-to-fermion kernels, and energy-momentum-tensor overlaps reproduce the known one-loop photon gravitational form factors $F_1$, $F_2$, and $F_3$. Our result provides an analytic benchmark for fermionic orbital and spin--orbit structure in the real photon.

papers.title: GNoF: A Low-SM-Overhead GPU-Native NVMe-over-Fabrics Completion Path for Data-Intensive GPU Workloads
papers.abstract: GPUs are the main compute engine for data-intensive workloads whose datasets exceed device memory and reside on remote flash. The conventional host CPU orchestrates every NVMe-over-Fabrics (NVMe-oF) transaction and stages data through host memory, costing high CPU usage, repeated CPU-GPU synchronization, and redundant data movement. GPU-initiated storage removes the CPU from the I/O path, but existing designs leave two problems: synchronous lock-step completion pins streaming multiprocessors (SMs) in spin-polling, wasteful over a 10-100 microsecond RDMA round trip, and current GPU-native remote systems focus on target-side firmware while using per-command doorbells and periodic CQ polling. We present GNoF, a GPU-native NVMe-oF/RDMA data path where GPU threads build command capsules, post send work-queue elements, ring doorbells, and reap completions entirely on the device; the CPU only handles one-time connection setup, the admin queue, and a keep-alive thread. Three mechanisms target long fabric round trips: a doorbell mover that coalesces a burst's doorbells into one MMIO ring; a batched CQ poller with a lock-free fast peek and monotonic completion counters that cannot lose a wakeup; and a set-associative, reference-pinned GPU page cache with split fetch/wait pipelining and orphan-fill takeover. GNoF needs no target or firmware change and runs against an unmodified SPDK target. On a 200 Gb/s InfiniBand fabric, GNoF reaches 1.77 million 4 KB IOPS per client at 0.37% host CPU and about 1% SM occupancy, versus 40% CPU for kernel nvme-rdma and about 100% SM occupancy for lock-step polling. Against three existing baselines (kernel nvme-rdma, BaM over a BlueField-3 DPU, and BaM on a local SSD) under identical workloads, we show 10-22x gains on selective column I/O, CPU-burn immunity, and the regime where bulk staging is faster.

papers.title: Connecting Extended Modal Dependence Logics
papers.abstract: We consider three natural extensions of the basic decidable dependence logic LFD, adding, respectively, conditional dependence atoms, independence atoms, and identity atoms between variables. We show that these systems are all connected to first-order logic with identity by SAT reductions and in several cases also faithful translations. In particular, this implies that all these extended modal-style dependence logics are undecidable. This solves a number of problems left open in the original publication [1] introducing the LFD framework. The definitions and proofs presented here were found by ChatGPT and checked and streamlined as needed by the authors. At the end, we provide some discussion of what new things we learnt about dependence logics and about the methodology of using AI in logical research.

papers.title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
papers.abstract: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

papers.title: The Price of Not Planning: Parallel Sampling Depth Peaks at the Reconstruction Threshold
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models sample the tokens of one round independently. Planned decoders first generate a coarse plan, then fill in the tokens in parallel. We ask when a plan saves rounds, how many it saves, and how fine it must be. We study this on broadcast trees: the leaves are the tokens, the internal nodes are the plan, and the edge correlation $\theta$ sets how strongly tokens depend on the plan. Errors are measured by the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence $\varepsilon$, and the lower bounds hold for every deterministic value-adaptive rule, also with learned conditionals. We show that a decoder without the plan needs of order $\min\{n,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds below the reconstruction threshold, where $\alpha=\log b/(4\log(1/\theta))$ rises to $1/2$ at the threshold, and that the exponent stays below $1/2$ above it (binary channel: $0.02\le\theta\le0.98$). With the plan, $\log_b n+1$ rounds suffice. In the binary model below the threshold, a plan with units of $m$ tokens needs of order $\log_b(n/m)+\min\{m,(n/\varepsilon)^{\alpha}\}$ rounds, so it gives logarithmic depth exactly when $m$ is logarithmic. A plan therefore helps most near the threshold, and only if its units are small. Exact divergence computations in the Gaussian model with up to $2^{20}$ leaves confirm these exponents below the threshold.

papers.title: Third-body-corrected Two-Pion Femtoscopic Correlations in Au+Au Collisions at High Baryon Density
papers.abstract: Identical charged pion femtoscopy provides a sensitive probe of the space-time structure of particle-emitting sources in heavy-ion collisions. At high baryon density, the differences between $\pi^+\pi^+$ and $\pi^-\pi^-$ Hanbury Brown--Twiss (HBT) radii may originate from both the third-body Coulomb effect and the initial-state isospin asymmetry. Since the latter is related to the equation of state (EoS) of asymmetric nuclear matter, separating these two effects is essential. In these proceedings, we present the measurements of identical charged pion correlations in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=3.0$, 3.2, 3.5, 3.9, 4.5, and 7.7 GeV collected by the STAR experiment. A correction procedure is developed to remove the residual third-body Coulomb effect. After correction, the extracted HBT radii of $\pi^+\pi^+$ and $\pi^-\pi^-$ become consistent within uncertainties. The results indicate that the observed charge dependence is dominated by the third-body Coulomb effect, while any remaining contribution from the initial-state isospin asymmetry to the relative HBT radius difference, $(R_{\pi^-}-R_{\pi^+})/R_{\pi^+}$, is constrained to be less than 5\% at the 95\% confidence level.

papers.title: PLECTA: Overlap-aware instance segmentation of dense strand networks from binary masks
papers.abstract: Many materials and tissues, including carbon-nanotube sheets, collagen and paper, comprise overlapping strands whose arrangement influences their effective properties. Measuring this geometry from micrographs requires individual strands to be traced through crossings and signal gaps, which merge distinct strands or split one strand into disconnected fragments. We present PLECTA (from Latin plecta, a braid), a deterministic method that segments individual strands using only a binary image whose foreground pixels mark strand centrelines. At each junction, PLECTA selects which strand segments continue into one another while allowing segments to terminate. It formulates this decision as an exact maximum-weight partial-matching problem, with an explicit penalty for unpaired segments and no restriction on the number of segments entering a junction. The output permits crossing pixels to belong to multiple strands. On synthetic scenes, PLECTA resolved strand identities more accurately than three released alternatives at every density tested. The same ranking held on an independently published generator run at its own settings. A separate stage uses the corresponding greyscale micrograph to estimate which strand lies on top at each crossing. The complete workflow is demonstrated on scanning electron micrographs of carbon nanotube sheets, from raw images to individual strand instances with estimated crossing order, without manual annotations for training or as pipeline inputs.

papers.title: How to calculate temperature and energy in Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation of the dynamics of classical objects has become incredibly popular in natural sciences since the method was developed in the sixties. A conservative estimate is that it involves many hundreds of thousands of scientific articles and all subdisciplines of natural sciences.
