Together, the simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, while remaining failures highlight opportunities to improve grounding, approach planning, and runtime.

papers.title: "Don't Leave the Task Unfinished": Persistence-Driven Violations under Quiet Oversight
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly given long, multi-step tasks to carry out, with the user reviewing little of what happens in between. Persistence, the tendency to keep working until a task is complete, is installed on purpose to improve performance on long tasks. Long-horizon tasks are typically complex, and the user's instruction can fall short of what the work actually requires, or conflict with the constraints the agent encounters in the task. We study what persistence does on long-horizon operations tasks that cannot be solved without breaking a documented constraint. We find that the agent pursues completion to the point of violating the constraint, and that a critically engaged user lowers the violation rate. Persistence takes violations from 29.2% to 58.3% across four models. Violations stay high wherever oversight goes quiet, whether the user is silent, assenting, or delegating with expressed trust. Only a questioning user, who asks for the basis of each action before allowing the next, brings the rate back to roughly the level measured without persistence. Practitioners should treat high persistence as a setting that carries a safety cost, and should recognize that the cost appears when oversight goes quiet. Safety here is better cast as a property of the human-AI pair than of the model alone. Project page: this https URL

papers.title: Chirality-polarized superradiance induced by quantized orbital-angular-momentum transfer in a ring cavity
papers.abstract: We investigate a spin-$1/2$ Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to two counterpropagating modes of an optical ring cavity and driven by Laguerre-Gaussian Raman beams carrying quantized orbital angular momentum (OAM). We demonstrate that competition between OAM-selective Raman scattering channels controls collective superradiance through self-consistent atom--cavity feedback, linking atomic orbital motion to cavity-chirality selection. For unequal OAM transfer, one cavity mode dominates the superradiant response, with its chirality switchable by the Raman pump strengths. In contrast, equal OAM transfer allows both counterpropagating modes to coexist. The resulting chirality-polarized phases support distinct vortex and vortex--antivortex configurations with reconstructed synthetic gauge-field textures. Remarkably, contact interactions can reshape the vortex topology without changing the dominant cavity chirality, revealing distinct responses of atomic and photonic degrees of freedom. The predicted mode switching and vortex ordering can be probed through cavity output and spin-resolved imaging in a proposed $^{87}$Rb implementation. Our results establish quantized OAM transfer as a mechanism for controlling collective cavity emission beyond conventional atomic SOAMC.

papers.title: Variance Stable Gaussian Smoothing Estimator for Arbitrary High-order Derivatives
papers.abstract: Computing high-order partial derivatives in high dimensions by automatic differentiation can be costly in both computation and memory. Stein's identity offers an alternative through Gaussian smoothing, but the variance of the resulting estimators can diverge as the step size tends to zero, even with antithetic sampling. We propose a variance stabilization technique that extends antithetic sampling from a reflection pair to $n$ equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane. Under local analyticity, we prove that, when $n$ is at least the derivative order, the bias is of order $O(\sigma^n)$ and the variance remains bounded as the smoothing step size $\sigma$ tends to zero. Numerical experiments support these predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the estimator in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for polyharmonic and Cahn--Hilliard equations. The technique mitigates the bias-variance trade-off in smoothing-based derivative estimation and is useful for PINNs solving high-order partial differential equations.

papers.title: The maximum length of a Hamiltonian path in the grid graph $P_m \times P_n$
A remark on the entropy numbers of mixed smoothness classes
Magnetic fields in blazar jets derived from synchrotron self-absorption
papers.abstract: Context. Magnetic fields are believed to play a crucial role in the launching, acceleration, and evolution of blazar jets. However, direct measurements of the magnetic field strength in the radio-emitting regions of blazar jets remain limited. Aims. We aim to estimate the magnetic field strengths in the synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) regions of blazar jets and investigate their connections with the properties of the jet and central engine. Methods. We compiled multifrequency radio data for 143 blazars and fitted their radio spectra with a combined power-law and SSA model to derive the turnover frequency and turnover flux density. The magnetic field strengths were then calculated by combining the SSA parameters with the very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measured angular sizes and Doppler factors compiled from the literature. Results. The SSA-derived magnetic fields are systematically lower than those obtained from broadband spectral energy distribution modeling, suggesting that the two methods probe different regions of the jet. We further investigated the correlations between the SSA magnetic field strength and the apparent knot speed, {\gamma}-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and accretion disk luminosity. Only a weak correlation is found between the SSA magnetic field strength and {\gamma}-ray luminosity, while the best-fit relations with the other investigated parameters also exhibit negative slopes, suggesting a common tendency that is qualitatively consistent with magnetic energy being progressively converted into bulk kinetic energy during jet propagation. Conclusions. Our work presents a large statistical studies of SSA-derived magnetic fields in blazars and provides new observational constraints on the magnetic evolution of relativistic jets.

papers.title: HEmIF-Bench: Benchmarking H&E-to-mIF Models BeyondVirtual-StainFidelity
papers.abstract: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-to-multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish downstream utility. We present HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen generators across eight datasets spanning molecular, cellular, tissue, and patient scales. HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs, benchmarking both against the pathology foundation reference UNI2. Mirroring the clinical workflow where pathologists rely on mIF to define cell phenotypes, delineate tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and germinal centers (GCs), and stratify patient risk, we evaluate external CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, dense nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and patient survival prediction. Across the benchmark, foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among the generators, while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths. Comparing the two routes reveals that internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, and larger output marker panels do not guarantee stronger downstream utility across datasets. Moreover, neither internal encoder features nor generated outputs consistently surpass frozen UNI2. These findings show that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream utility, and that generators trained at current paired-data scales have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models. With the expansion of paired translation cohorts and the advancement of foundation-based generative architectures, HEmIF-Bench establishes a definitive benchmark for tracking when H&E-to-mIF generation crosses the threshold to deliver genuine value beyond routine histology for tumor microenvironment analysis and precision oncology.

papers.title: DiffWAM: Learning World Action Model from Consecutive Visual Difference
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.

papers.title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
papers.abstract: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

papers.title: A simple proof of the characterization of $\ell_\infty^n$ by norm-one projections and a stability estimate
Remember, Replay, Adapt: Learning from Past Experience in Online Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

papers.title: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

papers.title: Towards the LSST DESC pipeline for cosmology with galaxy clusters -- design and validation on simulations
papers.abstract: We present the current implementation of an automated framework developed within the Legacy Survey of Space and Time Dark Energy Science Collaboration (LSST DESC) for galaxy cluster cosmology, in preparation for the first LSST data releases of the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The cluster cosmology pipeline integrates DESC-developed tools dedicated to galaxy/cluster catalog ingestion, cluster number count and weak lensing measurements, modeling, and parameter inference through posterior sampling, enabling reproducible end-to-end cluster cosmology analyses. We test and validate the pipeline using synthetic mock datasets and the LSST DESC cosmoDC2 simulation, performing a joint analysis of redMaPPer cluster abundance and stacked weak lensing profiles measured in bins of redshift and richness. We constrain two cosmological parameters, $\Omega_c$ and $\sigma_8$, along with six cluster mass-observable relation parameters. Our baseline analysis recovers the fiducial cosmoDC2 values of $\Omega_c$ and $\sigma_8$ within $0.51\sigma$ and $0.34\sigma$, respectively. We also showcase the flexibility of the overall pipeline by assessing the impact of fiducial cosmology and alternative modeling prescriptions on the parameter constraints. Lastly, we also discuss the current limitations of the pipeline and the developments needed for LSST data.

papers.title: Minimal sets of countable group actions on regular curves
HIVE-ECIA: Identity-Aware Historical Evidence Acquisition for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Object Tracking
papers.abstract: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360° field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.

papers.title: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.

papers.title: Diagonal and Fine Tower Dimensions for Minimal Circle Homeomorphisms and Product Actions
EasyNav: A Modular Architecture for Real-Time Navigation Across Heterogeneous Robot Environments
papers.abstract: Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios, where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and evolve at different rates. This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping, localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.

papers.title: Restoring Fair Hrtick Re-arming After Same-Task Repicks in the Linux EEVDF Scheduler
papers.abstract: Linux uses one-shot high-resolution scheduler ticks (hrticks) to request rescheduling at fair-class execution boundaries. We analyze a gap in the dispatch path in which an expired fair hrtick is not restarted when the fair scheduler selects the current task again. The gap arises because the same-task fast path bypasses set_next_task_fair(), the location that normally records the next fair hrtick delay. We introduce SNT_REPICK, an explicit same-task activation type for struct sched_class. For fair tasks, it preserves the fast path while restarting the hrtick from refreshed EEVDF state. For SCHED_DEADLINE, it deliberately performs no hrtick restart because the corresponding runtime state is not refreshed on a repick. The implementation was merged into the mainline Linux kernel as commit c72945693b. We give a conditional timing analysis for systems on which the periodic scheduler tick remains active and report validation from two platforms. Functional tests on an 80-core Ampere Altra exercised fair hrtick, deadline hrtick, and the CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS=n fallback. Independently, Intel's 0-Day Kernel Test Service reported a 34.2% increase in its stress-ng.rawudp.packets_32_bytes_received_per_sec metric on a 192-thread Intel Xeon 6740E under the documented test configuration. We distinguish this reported benchmark result from causal claims that require separate scheduler and network instrumentation.

papers.title: Frege's logic in Grundgesetze is nonclassical
Exact multiplicity for a Minkowski-curvature Neumann problem with a step weight
Antisymmetry Breaking for Critical Poincaré-Sobolev Extremals in the Three Dimensional Ball
Illusion of Explainability: A Sanity Check for Spectral Band Attribution in Satellite Time-Series Crop Classification
papers.abstract: Attribution methods are commonly validated through convergence across methods and consistency with domain knowledge, yet neither criterion establishes whether identified features are necessary for a task. This limitation is particularly relevant in multispectral remote sensing, where overlapping spectral information makes individual bands potentially substitutable. We investigate this gap in crop-type classification using GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, and Occlusion on a U-TAE segmentation model trained on Sentinel-2 time series from the PASTIS benchmark. All three methods identify vegetation-sensitive spectral regions consistent with domain knowledge, while Shapley and Occlusion exhibit strong ordering sensitivity in deletion and insertion tests. However, these properties do not reliably predict retraining performance. Aggregate attribution consensus masks substantial per-class disagreement, with pairwise mean Spearman correlations ranging from 0.09 to 0.79. Models retrained from scratch using the five lowest-ranked bands perform comparably to or better than those using the five highest-ranked bands. Furthermore, attribution rankings from an independently trained model with identical configuration and seed identify a different top-five subset that yields better retraining performance. Analysis of all 252 five-band subsets reveals consistently low effective dimensionality (1.35 to 2.62), suggesting substantial spectral redundancy. These findings demonstrate that plausible and apparently faithful attribution rankings do not necessarily identify task-relevant bands for improved retrained performance, highlighting the limitations of band-level feature attribution in spectrally redundant input spaces.

papers.title: Metallic or insulating magnetic phases of transition-metal oxides in light of the Slater vs Mott controversy
papers.abstract: Magnetic d-electron oxides usually have a long-range-ordered ground state and an above-ground-state disordered para phase. The historical Slater-Mott controversy still reverberating to date pertains to understanding the origin of the insulating vs metallic nature of these two phases. Slater suggested that the insulating character evolved from the long-range order (LRO) antiferromagnetic (AFM) cell-doubling, leading to energy band repulsion and thus to forming a band gap. The reliance on LRO to explain gapping suggests that the absence of LRO in the spin-disordered para-phase would deprive the system from band repulsion, thus predicting a metallic paramagnetic (PM) phase. This, however, conflicts with numerous current observations. The alternative Mott-Peierls-Hubbard view abandons the mean-field-like band structure view emphasizing instead the local interelectronic repulsion U as a strong correlation signature of gapping both at the presence or absence of LRO. However, U is not an easily measured or calculated quantity in periodic systems, a situation often leading in practice to treating U as an adjustable parameter. The current work uses a parameter-free mean-field-like approach (Density Functional Theory, DFT), allowing energy-lowering symmetry breaking. This is done by considering local magnetic motifs as building blocks of the macroscopic AFM or PM phases. It is found that even when such motifs are isolated electronically from each other (i.e. vanishing LRO) by embedding them in quantum barriers (such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra surrounded locally by wide-gap MgO) they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. Thus, the origin of the band gaps in AFM or PM phases need not be LRO or strong correlation and can be understood within the mean-field-like band structure approach with symmetry breaking.

papers.title: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization
papers.abstract: We consider regularized nonconvex optimization over a closed convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, which involves a convex nonsmooth regularizer $r$ in the objective and $n$ smooth equality constraints. To find a near-KKT point of the problem, we propose a prox-linear first-order method, named as SEPi-Prox, based on a smoothed exact-penalty formulation. At each outer iteration of SEPi-Prox, a strongly convex prox-linear subproblem is formed and solved inexactly to a sufficient accuracy. Under a local non-singularity condition that is weaker than some other commonly used regularity conditions or constraint qualifications, SEPi-Prox finds an $\epsilon$-KKT point within $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls, matching the lower bound for unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We employ Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient method (APG) and a dual cutting-plane method (DCP) for the prox-linear subproblems. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_r$ denote the numbers of arithmetic operations of evaluating one first-order oracle and one proximal mapping of $r$ over $\mathcal{X}$, respectively. Then SEPi-Prox requires $\widetilde{O}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}\epsilon^{-2} + (dn + \mathcal{C}_r)\epsilon^{-5/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}((\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}} + dn^2 + n\mathcal{C}_r + n^{3.373})\epsilon^{-2})$ total arithmetic operations to produce an $\epsilon$-KKT point, respectively by using APG and DCP as the subsolver. The latter result is preferable when $n$ is small and nearly matches the optimal dependence on $\epsilon$. Numerical experiments on instances of the multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification demonstrate the efficiency of SEPi-Prox with both subsolvers.

papers.title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.

papers.title: An Exploration of Physical and Chemical Representation in Coarse-Grained, Machine-Learned Protein Models
papers.abstract: Machine-learned coarse-graining has emerged as a reliable framework for building protein models that accurately and efficiently sample their relevant conformational landscape. Existing studies assume a predefined map from full- to coarse-grained resolution. However, the choice of map strongly affects the quality of the models. Here, we study the dependence of system-specific machine-learned coarse-grained (MLCG) models across 7 mapping choices, spanning different resolutions and embedding types for coarse-grained beads. We show that resolution and chemical diversity do not always correlate with accuracy, and that accurate protein-specific models can be generated using minimal chemical diversity if the latent space representation of the system has high enough dimensionality.

papers.title: Mock Observations: Morphological Analysis of Galactic Bars in IllustrisTNG Simulations
papers.abstract: Galactic bars are important tracers of disk-galaxy evolution, yet reported bar fractions vary among observational studies and between observations and cosmological simulations. We compare bar statistics and properties in the IllustrisTNG simulations(TNG100 and TNG50 at z~0.1) with Sloan Digital Sky Survey(SDSS) galaxies at0.1<=z<=0.1264. We generate synthetic r-band TNG images,match SDSS observational conditions,and analyze mock TNG and real SDSS images using a common image-based framework of source segmentation,morphological classification, and isophotal ellipse fitting. For face-on late-type galaxies with log(M*/Msun)>10,the global bar fractions are 26.68+/-0.23%,24.96(-.76/+.78)%, and 13.42(-1.07/+1.15)% for SDSS,TNG100,and TNG50,respectively. TNG100 broadly agrees with SDSS over 10^10<~M*<~10^11.2Msun but shows a higher fbar at higher masses, whereas TNG50 remains lower than SDSS over most of10^10<~M*<~10^11.7Msun. Bulge-disk decompositions show fewer high-n bulges in TNG100 than in SDSS,particularly at high masses,but more in TNG50. These differences in bulge concentration may contribute to the different bar fractions. Bar length generally increases with stellar mass,and this trend depends little on the adopted bar-length definition. However, the outer ellipticity-decline estimator(R0.85max) yields systematically larger bar lengths than the ellipticity-peak estimator (R(eps,max)^bar). Massive TNG100 galaxies have more extended stellar disks than SDSS,which may contribute to their smaller relative bar lengths(Rbar/Re). Our results indicate that observational conditions,sample selection,and bar-identification methodology can affect the inferred bar fraction,emphasizing comparable observational conditions and analysis procedures in simulation-observation comparisons. Our SDSS measurements may underestimate the bar fraction relative to observations with higher spatial resolution.

papers.title: Growing length scales while approaching the glass transition
papers.abstract: Even after decades of research, the nature of the glass transition is controversially debated: Kinetic freezing phenomena, purely local strain-mediated effects, or collective phenomena including a hidden phase transition are usually discussed. In this work, we check reports on clusters of correlated particles in supercooled liquids which grow upon approaching the glass-transition. We specifically focus on dielectric studies providing approximate access to the four-point correlation function, which allows insight into the evolution of so-called amorphous order. Existing temperature-dependent data derived from the three-point correlation function or higher-order dielectric susceptibilities are modeled using the random first-order transition theory combined with the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann law. This ansatz enables detailed predictions concerning normalized correlation lengths or the number of correlated particles as function of temperature and fragility. It provides a good fit to the experimental data for all materials investigated, including network and molecular glass formers and polymers. We conclude that length scales and corresponding particle numbers determined by the different methods used are at least similar and closely related to those considered by the theory. Moreover, the model predictions on the fragility dependence of the number of correlated molecules are at least approximately fulfilled. Existing criticism concerning an apparent lack of criticality in the temperature dependence of experimental correlation lengths is discussed in terms of this fragility dependence: All available data are well consistent with a hidden phase transition which is best revealed for the most fragile liquids.

papers.title: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
Weighted bisections of triangle-free subcubic graphs
Instability of non-minimal critical points of Newton's equation with real analytic potentials
Exciton-polarons in monolayer semiconductors with drifting electrons
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the optical absorption of moderately doped two-dimensional semiconductors can be described in terms of exciton-polarons. In this picture, interactions between a photoexcited exciton and a Fermi sea of excess charge carriers split the exciton spectrum into a lower-energy attractive polaron branch and a higher-energy repulsive polaron branch. Due to the negligible in-plane momentum of photons, however, optical measurements probe only exciton-polarons near zero momentum, leaving their finite-momentum physics largely unexplored. Here we propose accessing this regime by measuring the absorption in the presence of an electric bias current. In effect, this displaces the electronic Fermi sea in momentum space, such that an optically active exciton-polaron at rest acquires finite momentum relative to the charge carriers. Using a diagrammatic formulation of the exciton-polaron problem, we derive exact relations between the spectral and quasiparticle properties of current-biased exciton-polarons and their finite-momentum counterparts in an equilibrium Fermi sea. These relations show that absorption measurements with drifting electrons can reconstruct the momentum dependence of the quasiparticle properties for both branches. We estimate that experimentally accessible currents can probe a broad momentum range while remaining within the linear-response regime.

papers.title: Quantum Startup, Recoil Statistics and Collective Gain in Free-Electron Lasers
papers.abstract: We examine the conditions under which quantum signatures can be distinguished from classical dynamics and statistical fluctuations in a free-electron laser. Starting from minimal coupling and the Bambini--Renieri frame, we derive the momentum-photon exchange Hamiltonian and its Raman-Nath ladder. An interaction-picture expansion retains detuning exactly and organizes recoil corrections through the mismatch between neighboring orders. Its validity depends on the accumulated recoil phase over the populated ladder, rather than on elementary recoil alone. Numerical checks and Gaussian entrance packets illustrate the effects of preparation and resonance averaging. We distinguish number-state exchange amplitudes from predictions for a coherent optical seed, and joint electron-field coherence from reduced radiation coherence. The Wigner representation connects finite recoil translations with classical transport and identifies the information required for bunching. A cavity channel then provides the basis for comparison with the recoil-resolved oscillator proposed by Kling and Giese, including the optical-undulator preparation, stimulated back-action and narrow resonance acceptance. Space charge, spontaneous diffusion and FEL-induced energy spread are compared with recoil and high-gain bandwidth scales. The coherent undulator pump is essential to exclude artificial zero-recoil antibunching from a number-state preparation. Startup and excess photon variance alone do not establish a quantum signature: the specified observable must remain distinguishable from a classical stochastic baseline under compatible preparation, propagation and detection conditions.

papers.title: Free energy profile computations for force-induced melting of a short B-DNA using Jarzynski equality
papers.abstract: We initially equilibrate a system of solvated 12-base pair canonical B-DNA of a specified sequence in a state of no external force acting on it (state $A: f=0$). A switching experiment is then performed by pulling one end of the DNA while restraining its other end. The pulling force is taken up to a maximum of 400 pN (state $B$), at a specified constant rate. The non-equilibrium work done W associated with this finite-time process is determined by integrating the extension of the DNA molecule with respect to the applied force. The distribution of the work values $P(W)$ is obtained by repeating the pulling process several times, wherein each time, the process is started with macroscopic state $A$. The free energy profile $\Phi(f)$ is obtained by a suitably devised method from the Jarzynski equality. The conformational space of the DNA is also sampled in an equilibrium method of umbrella sampling by considering the end-to-end length $\xi$ as the reaction coordinate. The associated potential of mean force (PMF) $\Phi(\xi)$ is then computed by invoking the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM). From the results, we observe that the equilibrium free energy difference between two states, $A$ and $B$, $\Delta F_{AB} ~(=F_B -F_A)$ obtained through both methods, is in close agreement with each other, despite the differences along the profiles $\Phi(f)$ and $\Phi(\xi)$, attributed to their distinct pathways of unzipping.

papers.title: Large Language Model-based Optimization for Wireless Communication: A Survey
papers.abstract: The growing complexity and dynamism of modern wireless communication frameworks have made real-time optimization essential for efficient resource allocation. Traditional optimization and machine-learning techniques often struggle with generalization, adaptability, stability, and scalability in heterogeneous, time-varying environments. Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools capable of reasoning over structured prompts and generating context-aware decisions in real time without domain-specific retraining. This survey provides a comprehensive review of LLM-driven optimization techniques applied to wireless communication problems such as power control, bandwidth allocation, task offloading, and intelligent surface configuration. We introduce a functional taxonomy of LLM-enabled wireless resource management strategies and analyze the prompt engineering methodologies employed in recent literature. Furthermore, we develop a generalized analytical framework that categorizes LLM-based optimization architectures, including direct solution generation, closed-loop optimization with external verifiers, and representation encoding within trainable neural pipelines. To demonstrate practical applicability, we present representative case studies on LLM-assisted beam prediction for millimeter-wave systems and adaptive wireless resource allocation. Finally, we discuss emerging hybrid AI approaches for wireless networks.

papers.title: Let Execution Do the Teaching
papers.abstract: Improving a coding model is a sequence of decisions: find the limiting behavior, create useful practice, and determine which attempts deserve reinforcement. We investigate a practical way to make those decisions increasingly repeatable by grounding feedback in execution. Starting from GLM-4.7-Flash, the work combines whole-file supervised fine-tuning, targeted C++ repair curricula, group-relative reinforcement learning, and verifiers that turn program behavior into structured rewards. Compiler errors and failing tests provide specific contexts for repair practice, while executable checks score the resulting programs. We evaluate the trained models on 26 C++ coding tasks, measuring both initial success and completion after test feedback. The strongest reported post-training configuration achieves 45.2% success in the first test round and 61.5% within two rounds. These results come from an assisted development suite with evolving prompt contracts; the strongest configuration uses four selected evaluation trials and includes six tasks also used in training. The study describes an execution-guided workflow for improving coding models, including how repair tasks are constructed, how program behavior determines rewards, and how the resulting models are evaluated.

papers.title: A Negative Answer to a Variant of the Lins-de Melo-Pugh Conjecture
Uniqueness of limit cycle{s} in a class of classical trinomial Liénard systems
Who Writes the Codebook? An Eight-Step Framework for Auditing LLM-Generated Category Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly create the categories through which qualitative evidence is interpreted. Existing coding benchmarks often hold these categories fixed. We propose the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method that compares codebook creation, repeated application and code distributions under controlled inputs. It combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to distinguish variation in the overall pipeline from application differences within a common category system. An application to 668 organisational interviews, 13,166 text units and eight models from five vendors yields 48 codebooks and 270 coding runs. Models create markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from .76 to .92, whereas between-model agreement on the shared codebook is about .69. The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies before substantive interpretation. It assesses reliability and representational consequences, not interpretive validity or the quality of resulting theory.

papers.title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

papers.title: Toward an Admissibility Theory of Aharonov--Bohm Arbitrage
Theory of anisotropic magnetotransport beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation in multi-Weyl semimetals
papers.abstract: Multi-Weyl semimetals, characterized by Weyl nodes carrying higher monopole charges, provide a platform for exploring topological magnetotransport beyond the conventional Weyl paradigm. Here, we develop a generalized semiclassical Boltzmann framework for multi-Weyl semimetals with arbitrary monopole charge $N$, incorporating the orbital magnetic moment (OMM) into the quasiparticle dispersion and Berry-curvature-modified dynamics, together with a momentum-dependent collision integral accounting for intra- and intervalley scattering. We investigate the longitudinal magnetoconductivity (LMC) and planar Hall conductivity (PHC) for $N=1$, $2$, and $3$, considering both nonmagnetic and magnetic impurity scattering. In the absence of OMM, the LMC remains positive and quadratic in the magnetic field throughout the investigated scattering regime, consistent with conventional chiral-anomaly-assisted transport. Including OMM, however, leads to a sign reversal of the LMC under sufficiently strong intervalley scattering for the $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_z$ impurity channels. Remarkably, the critical intervalley scattering strength decreases systematically with increasing monopole charge, indicating an enhanced tendency toward negative LMC in higher-charge Weyl systems. Furthermore, we find that the PHC also undergoes a sign reversal for $N=2$ and $N=3$ in the same impurity channels, while remaining positive for $N=1$ within the investigated parameter range. The angular dependences retain their characteristic $\sin^2\gamma$-like and $\sin2\gamma$ profiles for LMC and PHC, respectively, even across the sign reversal. Our results demonstrate that the interplay of Berry curvature, OMM, monopole charge, and impurity scattering can produce qualitatively distinct weak-field magnetotransport responses beyond the conventional chiral-anomaly picture.

papers.title: HalluProbe: Exploiting VLM Hallucinations for Backdoor Detection
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.

papers.title: Stripped White Dwarfs as Spectroscopic Clocks: Abundance Transitions in Partial Tidal Disruptions
papers.abstract: We investigate partial tidal disruptions of He and CO white dwarfs (WDs) by a $10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. We construct realistic WD structures and abundance profiles with MESA and map them into FLASH to follow the remnant response and the time-dependent composition of the fallback debris in single pericentre passages on tightly bound orbits ($e=0.9$). The element-specific fallback rates exhibit pre-peak compositional transitions that trace the WD's stratified layers. In the grazing encounter ($\beta=0.55$), hydrogen dominates the earliest returning debris, followed by helium, showing a H$\rightarrow$He transition. Deeper encounters ($\beta=0.7$ and $0.8$) penetrate the CO core and produce a He$\rightarrow$C transition, that occurs earlier relative to peak fallback and is stronger in the deeper encounter. These signatures provide a potential spectroscopic diagnostic for identifying CO-WD tidal disruption events (TDEs). We then develop a semi-analytic model for repeated tidal stripping and predict passage-to-passage compositional evolution, in which the stripped material becomes progressively enriched in heavier elements as deeper layers are exposed, leading to stronger and earlier abundance transitions in later flares. We find that WDs can survive several dozen ($\sim 30$-$80$) passages, depending on their initial mass and compactness. Our results link time-dependent abundance signatures to repeating WD disruptions and provide testable observable predictions for identifying IMBH-powered transients.

papers.title: Uniquely balanced polyhedral complexes are highly connected
Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks (WPUSNs) allow underground devices (UDs) to harvest radio-frequency energy from a UAV via wireless energy transfer (WET) techniques, enabling sustainable Internet of underground things (IoUT) applications. This paper integrates rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA)-aided simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) into UAV-enabled WPUSNs to deliver information and energy to UDs. Within this framework, we investigate a max-min fairness problem that jointly optimizes the UAV transmit power, power allocation and message splitting, power-splitting ratios, and time allocation, aiming to maximize the minimum uplink throughput across UDs subject to per-UD downlink throughput requirements and a UAV energy-consumption constraint. To address this non-convex problem under dynamic underground environments, we develop an off-policy deep reinforcement learning approach based on the primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC), where a TQC-based reward critic evaluates the fairness objective, cost critics estimate constraint costs, and an actor learns the resource-control policy with adaptive dual-variable updates. Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements from a center-pivot irrigation farm demonstrate that PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput compared with four benchmarks while satisfying the per-frame constraints in over 96% of the evaluated frames, and that this throughput advantage is preserved under different Rician factors, numbers of UDs, and downlink throughput thresholds.

papers.title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
papers.abstract: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.

papers.title: Velocity weakening and stick-slip in mean-field depinning with stress overshoots
papers.abstract: We study a fully connected depinning model with transient stress overshoots of strength $M$, driven through a spring of stiffness $k_0$. Combining exact stationary relations, linear stability analysis, direct simulations, and population dynamics, we connect the force--velocity characteristic to stick-slip motion and quasistatic avalanche statistics. For $M>1$, two distinct stiffness scales organize the response. At $k_0=k_{\rm w}\equiv M-1$, the stationary characteristic first develops a velocity-weakening branch, whereas $k_0=k_{\rm q}\equiv(M-1)^2/(4M)$ marks the onset of finite-amplitude stick-slip in the quasistatic limit. Their separation produces an intermediate regime in which the quasistatic force converges to a stationary value, whereas finite-velocity driving produces stick-slip below a critical velocity. Quasistatic avalanches in this regime undergo transient amplification and display an excess of large, asymmetric events---"ghost kings"---that remain finite. By contrast, at and below $k_{\rm q}$ the same amplification produces system-spanning "genuine kings" and a finite quasistatic force cycle. These results show how elastic loading dynamically selects among the branches of a reentrant force--velocity relation and clarify the connection between velocity weakening, stick-slip, and runaway avalanches.

papers.title: Bioformer-RetroMAE: retrieval-oriented pretraining of a compact biomedical language model for literature search
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval is increasingly used for biomedical literature search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Most biomedical bi-encoders are built on BERTBase-sized encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (MLM). These encoders are costly for corpus-scale indexing and latency-sensitive query encoding, and MLM does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector that a bi-encoder uses to represent a whole text. We present Bioformer-RetroMAE, a compact (43M-parameter) retrieval-oriented biomedical encoder obtained by continually pretraining Bioformer8L} with RetroMAE on approximately 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts. After bi-encoder fine-tuning with BM25 hard negatives, we evaluated it on BioASQ Task 12B test questions by retrieving from all PubMed abstracts. Bioformer-RetroMAE outperformed BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders fine-tuned under identical settings on all metrics, despite having about 40% of their parameters and producing 512-dimensional rather than 768-dimensional vectors. Compared with PubMedBERT, it improved mean average precision (MAP) by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1%. Compared with the original Bioformer8L}, RetroMAE pretraining improved MAP by 53.6% and Recall@100 by 32.8% without changing model size or inference cost. In hybrid retrieval, fusing Bioformer-RetroMAE with BM25 through weighted reciprocal rank fusion improved MAP and NDCG@10 over BM25 alone by 4.9% and 4.6%, respectively, larger gains than those obtained by fusing BM25 with PubMedBERT or BioBERT.

papers.title: HBF-EventLab: A Discrete-Event Simulator for Studying Host-Device Coordination in High Bandwidth Flash
papers.abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) combines NAND flash density with high-bandwidth accelerator connectivity, offering additional memory capacity for large language model inference. However, limited hardware availability makes it difficult to evaluate how host behavior and device resource constraints jointly affect HBF request processing. We present HBF-EventLab, an open-source, transaction-level discrete-event simulator based on the Open Compute Project HBF specification. HBF-EventLab connects host request dispatch, command admission, fragmented write assembly, read dispatch, NAND execution, and completion feedback within a shared event loop. It explicitly models distinct resource lifetimes and separates configurable scheduling policies from ordering and resource constraints, enabling controlled exploration of host-device coordination. Experiments show how resource limits, address interleaving, fragment arrival patterns, and scheduling policies affect write completion and request latency. The results highlight the need to consider resource limits and scheduling policies jointly, accounting for their interactions with write assembly and read eligibility. We also integrate HBF-EventLab with real GPU execution of Qwen3-0.6B, combining profiled GPU activity durations with simulated weight-access delays to estimate time to first token and time per output token, with logits and output tokens remaining bitwise identical to those from native GPU execution. HBF-EventLab provides a configurable foundation for studying HBF mechanisms, exploring scheduling policies, and assessing how HBF access delays affect application-level timing. The source code is publicly available at this https URL .

papers.title: Optimisation of gas mixture for charge and light readout with Micromegas detectors
papers.abstract: Optical readout of Micromegas detectors is a promising technique for neutron and charged-particle imaging, offering high spatial resolution while reducing the complexity of electronic readout. Within the framework of the development of optical-readout Micromegas detectors, different noble-gas-based mixtures have been investigated to optimize charge amplification and scintillation yield. Argon-, neon-, and helium-based mixtures with various quenchers were characterized using X-ray irradiation. The detector gain, energy resolution, and optical light intensity were measured simultaneously over a wide range of amplification fields. Unprecedented energy resolutions were achieved over a large detection area (several cm$^2$) with He/\CF and Ne/\CF (90/10) mixtures, reaching 10.5\% and 13.3\% (FWHM), respectively, with the He-based mixture delivering particularly remarkable performance. Simultaneous charge and optical measurements further reveal that high charge gain does not necessarily translate into a strong optical response: while He- and Ne-based mixtures achieve effective charge gains of the order of 10$^5$, Ar/\CF mixtures produce the strongest detected light signals. Among the investigated mixtures, the ternary Ar/\CF/Isobutane (95/3/2) mixture stands out as particularly promising, combining high effective charge gain, a comparatively strong optical response, and more stable detector operation.

papers.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
papers.abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

papers.title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
papers.abstract: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

papers.title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models
papers.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.

papers.title: On $ι$Quiver (BPS) Algebras and (Strict) Partitions
papers.abstract: We consider the $\iota$quiver algebras of split type associated with the quiver BPS algebras of affine type A. They are supposed to give twisted affine Yangians and (elliptic) $\iota$quantum toroidal algebras that could possibly arise from D-branes on $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^2/\mathbb{Z}_n$ with orientifolds. We mention some properties of these algebras, such as the minimalistic presentations in the rational cases and the coideal structures. We also investigate how one might identify these algebras from the quiver theories with orientifold actions. Moreover, we discuss some representations with combinatorial bases of these algebras. In particular, the algebras with $n=1,2$ in certain limits of the parameters have representations labelled by (coloured) strict/symmetric partitions, which in the case of $n=1$ recovers the known BPS counting of certain theories.

papers.title: Scaling Fourier Inequalities for Locally Compact Quantum Groups
Indication of demographic and epidemiological data on early-stage risks and long-term epidemic burden
papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between age-specific cumulative infection burden and the probability of triggering a major outbreak in heterogeneous populations. We develop two modeling frameworks that incorporate empirical age-stratified contact matrices: a deterministic framework for deriving the final size relation and a stochastic framework based on a Continuous-time Markov chain epidemic model, for which a multi-type branching-process approximation is used to characterize early-stage outbreak risk. The framework is illustrated using empirical social contact data from Guangzhou, Foshan, and Zhuhai, China, under two disease-motivated scenarios representing COVID-19 and hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). The illustrative analyses indicate that the relationship between cumulative infection burden and early-stage outbreak risk depends on both epidemiological characteristics and population contact patterns. In particular, age groups with the highest final attack rates do not necessarily have the highest probability of triggering a major outbreak. These findings highlight the complementary nature of the two measures and the value of considering both when assessing age-specific epidemic risks in practice.

papers.title: Electrical transport of surface-bound electrons on annealed solid neon
papers.abstract: We study the dc transport of electrons bound to the surface of solid neon using the conventional Sommer-Tanner method. First, we find that the capacitive cross-talk for the thickness of solid samples on the order of a millimeter varies substantially with the temperature and is strongly affected by the sample annealing. Second, we find that, even for the annealed samples, the observed response of electrons differs significantly from that of the surface-bound electrons on liquid helium and cannot be satisfactorily described by conventional models. Despite this, we managed to extract the resistance of the electron system from its in-phase response and investigate the temperature dependence in a wide range between 1.4 and 20 K. In a high-temperature range between 16 and 20 K, the resistance behavior is found to agree very well with the vapor-atom scattering mechanism, while at lower temperatures it is consistent with temperature-dependent scattering by surface roughness. Our analysis indicates a high electron mobility of electrons on solid neon but two orders of magnitude lower density than expected. These results suggest surface electrons as a suitable probe for studying the morphology of the neon surface but call for a better understanding of the experimental method applicable to such systems.

papers.title: Sparse Stabilization of Continuous-Time Linear Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Efficient use of communication resources is crucial for stabilizing a networked control system. Employing \emph{sparse inputs} and event-triggered control are efficient ways to utilize communication resources in networked control systems. This work considers the problem of stabilizing a continuous-time linear dynamical system (LDS) using $s$-sparse inputs. For this purpose, we consider \emph{switched} linear feedback control, where we construct a finite number of feedback matrices with at most $s$ nonzero rows. Using switched systems theory, we show that there exists an $s$-sparse input for any sparsity level $s \geq 1$ that ensures stability when the continuous-time LDS is stabilizable. In addition, using our approach, we can compute the required feedback matrices with minimal overhead even if the sparsity budget $s$ varies over time. We also minimize the maximum Frobenius norm of the feedback matrices, yielding sparse inputs with reduced control energy. We show that an upper bound on the control energy required for stabilization using an $s$-sparse input is inversely proportional to $s^2$, while maintaining the same exponential stability rate. Finally, we combine the design of the \emph{sparse inputs} with the event-trigger rule to further reduce communication resource consumption. Our sparse and event-triggered control strategy ensures that any stabilizable continuous-time LDS can be stabilized using $s$-sparse inputs under both state feedback and output feedback, for any $s\geq 1$. We illustrate our theoretical results for the task of stabilizing a mass-spring system.

papers.title: Record-proof optical communication enabled by a quantum receiver with lossless optical decryption
papers.abstract: We propose record-proof physical-layer encryption (PLE) based on quantum-optimal reception. Unlike conventional symmetric-key encryption algorithms, the proposed scheme prevents decryption of recorded signals even if the secret key is disclosed after transmission. Existing PLE schemes rely on practical limitations of the eavesdropper's receiver in pursuing record-proof security; ours instead exploits the noncommutativity of conjugate optical quadratures to give the legitimate receiver an intrinsic sensitivity advantage. A phase-controlled Kennedy receiver performs lossless optical decryption and near-optimal binary-state discrimination. We demonstrate record-proof security with a 3.0-dB channel-loss budget, showing that quantum receivers offer cryptographic functions beyond sensitivity enhancement.

papers.title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

papers.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
papers.abstract: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

papers.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
papers.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.

papers.title: Reflection Is Not Always Worth It: Budgeted Reflection Allocation for Recommendation Agents
papers.abstract: This work aims to make recommendation agents more efficient by reducing unnecessary LLM reflection while preserving full-catalog ranking and inference reranking. Since BRAVE changes only how training-time reflection is allocated, it does not introduce new user data requirements or additional LLM exposure beyond the base agent protocol. The main potential risk is that a poorly calibrated allocator may assign less reflection to users whose preferences are sparse, niche, or under-represented, which could weaken personalization for those users or indirectly affect item exposure. This risk can be mitigated through deployment-time auditing and conservative allocation design. In practice, reflection budgets should be evaluated not only by aggregate Recall or NDCG, but also across user-history lengths, item popularity groups, and application-relevant cohorts when such analysis is permitted. The allocator should rely on task-side ranking evidence rather than sensitive attributes, and fallback policies can reserve a small portion of the budget for random or fairness-aware coverage when subgroup robustness is important. Privacy risks can be controlled with the same protections required by the base recommendation agent: minimizing user text sent to the LLM controller, anonymizing user identifiers, retaining only necessary interaction evidence, and applying standard access-control and logging policies. Overall, BRAVE is designed as a cost-aware allocation layer, and its ethical deployment depends on validating that the saved computation does not come at the expense of vulnerable users or responsible exposure.

papers.title: Borel $(2n+1)$-coloring for bounded degree function graphs
Enhancing Exploration in Ensemble Kalman Inversion via Covariance Inflation and Projected Dropout
papers.abstract: Ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI) is a derivative-free and parallelizable method for parameter estimation in Bayesian inverse problems involving expensive forward models. It adapts Kalman filtering by repeatedly assimilating the observation data through an artificial dynamical system with identity state evolution and the parameter-to-observation map as its observation operator. However, its performance can be limited by ensemble collapse and confinement to the affine span of the initial ensemble. We propose an exploration-enhanced EKI framework that combines multiplicative covariance inflation with a projected-dropout correction of the ensemble mean. Inflation helps maintain ensemble spread, while projected dropout enables the mean to explore directions beyond the initial affine span. For linear inverse problems, we provide a discrete-time, finite-ensemble analysis of the resulting method and prove the least-squares objective converges exponentially to its minimum in expectation. Within the initial ensemble subspace, the contraction factor is independent of the conditioning of the inverse problem, and the limiting ensemble covariance provides a low-rank representation of the posterior covariance. Experiments on ill-conditioned linear systems, 100-dimensional nonlinear benchmarks, and a PDE-constrained barotropic flow inverse problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: A Speech-LLM Framework for Enrollment-Free Wake-Word-Guided Target-Speaker Recognition in Complex Noisy Scenarios for Seamless Human-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Target-speaker automatic speech recognition (TS-ASR) is essential for reliable human-machine interaction in complex acoustic environments, where overlapping speech and background noise make it difficult to identify and recognize the intended speaker. Existing approaches typically rely on speaker enrollment or cascaded processing pipelines, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. To address these limitations, we propose an enrollment-free Speech-LLM framework that leverages wake-word text as a lexical cue to guide target-speaker recognition.
