CSDX models of different parcellations were employed to explore the potential regulatory associations of brain connectome patterns and constituents of protein-protein interaction (PPI) cascades of hybrid assembly pathways of endogenous multiprotein complexes. Metrics of continuous engagement of the PPI cascade nucleated protein dimers of CORUM multiprotein complexes have been identified as statistical components of the multivariate transcriptome-connectome associations. It accounts for additional connectome associated variations beyond the five measured axes in the 82 nodes CSDX model. Comparisons of the seven arm models of transcriptome-connectome associations demonstrate that the mouse derived model generally fits the mouse brain connectome better, while the human derived model assigns a significantly larger fraction of its transcriptome-connectome association to unique rather than net shared contributions. This study nominates elite panels of top scoring candidate protein dimers and CORUM multiprotein complexes for follow up mechanistic studies of their potential roles in structural functional features governing mammalian brain connectome.

papers.title: Behavioral Denoising: A New Perspective on Nonlinear Behavioral Control Inspired by Closed-Form Diffusion Policies
papers.abstract: Diffusion policies have become a dominant approach to imitation learning in robotics. Recent work suggests that, in the low-data regime, they largely retrieve or combine the demonstrated actions, which the closed-form diffusion policy does explicitly. This closely resembles behavioral control, where future inputs are formed as linear combinations of recorded trajectories. In this work, we make this connection precise: we show that the weights with which the closed-form diffusion policy combines the demonstrated actions are the unique solution of a regularized behavioral control problem. Building on this connection, we propose an algorithm, termed $\chi^2$-projected behavioral denoising, which is a training-free method that combines nearby trajectory data with a limit on extrapolation when the data offer little support. It shows encouraging results on four nonlinear control tasks compared to recent nonlinear behavioral control methods. We hope that this connection offers a useful perspective for understanding both data-driven control and diffusion policies. Code and more visualizations can be found at this https URL .

papers.title: On Semi-interval and Para-interval Graphs
Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
papers.abstract: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

papers.title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.

papers.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study
papers.abstract: The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices that are easy to overlook: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient actually tests. We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study in which the same pipelines were applied to data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling. An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared under only one of the four pipelines, the one combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs, and was absent under the other three. More tellingly, that same pipeline reported a group difference in 40% of cases where none was present, almost always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. This shows that the same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on choices that are rarely reported. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

papers.title: The Akhmediev breather for the Dysthe equation and the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave
papers.abstract: In this article we define and compute the breather of the Dysthe equation for deep water waves, the analogue of the Akhmediev breather of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS). When a single pair of modes is unstable, the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave consists of the Stokes wave and the translates and time shifts of a single solution, the breather. The construction uses only gauge and translation invariance, not integrability or a Hamiltonian structure. We use the parameterisation method to find the breather as a power series whose coefficients follow recursively from linear equations. This is not an asymptotic expansion: the series is the Taylor series of the breather itself. For deep water waves we map the envelope amplification over steepness and group length and give a simple formula, based on the linear stability analysis, that summarises it to within a few per cent. Our results agree well with Euler simulations: the edge of the instability band of the Dysthe equation lies much closer to the onset of growth than that of the NLS, and, away from the onset and below breaking, the crest and height amplifications lie less than 5% below the Euler ones.

papers.title: MOUSSE: Multilingual Overlapped Speech Separation with Predictive Uncertainty Estimation
papers.abstract: Recent generative speech separation methods have shown promising performance, yet mixtures of overlapping speech in different languages remain underexplored. To this end, we first curate MuSSeD, an English-Korean benchmark comprising two- to four- speaker mixtures across varying overlap ratios. We further propose MOUSSE, a flow matching framework that incorporates boundary-aware training and frame-wise predictive uncertainty through a permutation-invariant Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The predicted scale is further used to adapt classifier-free guidance during sampling. MOUSSE achieves 13.18 dB SI-SDRi and 0.175 ESTOIi, outperforming discriminative and flow matching-based separation baselines, with a 1.58 dB SI-SDRi improvement over the strongest model.

papers.title: Ferroelectric control of the $K$--$Γ$ valley landscape in R-stacked bilayer WSe$_2$
papers.abstract: In bilayer WSe2 the valence-band maxima at K and {\Gamma} lie within a few thermal energies of one another, and gating redistributes holes between a light and a heavy valley of different mobilities on a landscape that stays fixed. We show that rhombohedral (R) stacking moves the landscape itself. The three-fold symmetry of R stacking forbids interlayer tunneling at K but not at {\Gamma}. The K coupling is therefore exactly zero, not merely small. A fit that leaves the coupling free returns an upper bound of 0.017 meV, three orders of magnitude under k_BT at room temperature, while the {\Gamma} coupling is 361.8 meV. The polarization creates a potential step between the layers and splits the K doublet. Each K state stays on a single layer, so the K edge shifts by half of that splitting, 41.7 meV, which any tunneling would reduce. {\Gamma} barely responds. Two consequences follow from symmetry alone, whatever the size of that shift. The two registries, carrying opposite out-of-plane ferroelectric polarizations, are exact mirror images along the displacement-field axis, and reversing the polarization reverses the displacement of the landscape. Their differential-mode transconductances are equal and opposite at zero field, where the response vanishes for an ideal nonpolar reference. The stored polarization is read out as a reversal of sign and not as a difference of current. Sweeping the field is a second route to the same parity. In the ideal symmetric limit the transconductance passes through zero at the field that cancels the polarization, 1.07 V/nm, at a single temperature. Both routes are limited by the symmetry of the device more than by the band structure. Stacking also renormalizes the landscape, so the polar one is not a translated copy of the nonpolar reference. Absolute offsets follow the exchange-correlation functional. The symmetry relations do not.

papers.title: The automorphism group of the super Jordan plane
Real-Time Air Pollution Monitoring and Tracking via Adaptive Density-Driven Multi-UAV Coordination
papers.abstract: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D$^2$C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D$^2$C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D$^2$C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D$^2$C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.

papers.title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
papers.abstract: We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

papers.title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

papers.title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
papers.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

papers.title: A simplified temporal logic completeness proof
papers.abstract: A temporal logic discussed in the author's book "Logics of Time and Computation" is given a simpler proof of semantic completeness, eliminating some flaws in the original.

papers.title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
papers.abstract: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

papers.title: SPIKE-Accelerated Split-Bregman/ADMM Methods for Obstacle Problems and American Option Pricing under Jump-Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents a parallel split Bregman/alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) \cite{goldstein,tran} for obstacle problems and for the linear complementarity problems (LCPs) that arise in the pricing of American options under the Black--Scholes and Merton jump-diffusion \cite{merton} models. The auxiliary variable of ADMM decouples the inequality constraint from the differential operator, so that every iteration consists of a linear solve with a fixed banded matrix and a pointwise projection. The matrix is factorized once by the SPIKE algorithm \cite{spike}, as in the parallel direct approach of \cite{singh}, and reused in all iterations and time steps in a Fortran~90 MPI implementation. Convergence is proved by a Lyapunov functional for every positive augmentation parameter, for the symmetric obstacle problem and the non-symmetric option LCP alike, and the iterates do not depend on the number of processes. The method therefore needs a single factorization, no tuned relaxation parameter and only pointwise, perfectly parallel updates. One- and two-dimensional obstacle problems, the Black--Scholes call and American put, and European and American options under Merton's model are computed and compared with exact, closed-form, binomial and published values. In two dimension a speed-up of $3.92$ on four processes is obtained. It is also shown that the augmentation parameter has to be scaled to the diagonal of the time-stepping matrix when only a few inner iterations are used.

papers.title: On Minima of 3D Lennard-Jones Lattice Energy and FCC-Tetragonal-Simple Hexagonal Phase Transitions
Equivalent-circuit analysis of the transverse resonant beam coupling impedance due to ceramic-chamber RF shields in the J-PARC Main Ring spill-feedback quadrupoles
papers.abstract: Ceramic vacuum chambers in fast-ramping or fast-response magnets are equipped with RF shields of conducting strips closed through lumped capacitors, which form a resonant circuit coupled to the transverse dipole moment of the beam. We evaluate the transverse beam coupling impedance due to the RF shields of the ceramic chambers in the spill-feedback quadrupole magnets of the J-PARC Main Ring. The RF shield is modelled by a magneto-quasi-static partial element equivalent circuit, and the laminated yoke of the magnet by a two-dimensional field solution with a complex permeability. The analysis shows a low-$Q$ resonant coupling impedance. The yoke lowers the resonance frequency and raises the shunt impedance per quality factor, and its effect cannot be neglected. The quality factor is determined mainly by the losses in the capacitors and in the laminations. The predicted peak impedance of the three chambers exceeds the resistive-wall impedance of the whole ring. The model can be applied to other machines and to the design of future rapid-cycling synchrotrons.

papers.title: Boundary regularity, finiteness and stability of energy-maximizing vortex patches
Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions
papers.abstract: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy. We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature. The database provides a systematic reference for metallic coherent heterophase interfaces and demonstrates the importance of separating strain and chemical energy contributions when interpreting alloy behavior.

papers.title: MathaMAGICal: Validating Trajectory Data Attribution During Capability Acquisition
papers.abstract: Influence-function-based methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores for trajectory data attribution, yet only retraining indicates whether those scores accurately predict data removal. We evaluate MAGIC on $86$M- and $152$M-parameter GPT-2-style models learning multistep arithmetic from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families. Full-run attribution at $86$M suffers from numerical overflow, and even with metagradient clipping, scores correlate near chance with retraining (linear datamodeling score, LDS, $0.17$--$0.22$). In contrast, short checkpoint windows yield stable, accurate predictions at both scales (LDS $0.86$--$0.99$ across four $100$-step windows at $152$M), whereas a single-checkpoint gradient-dot baseline shows near-zero correlation. Rankings of individual training blocks predict retraining only within that single run and do not transfer across seeds or hyperparameters ($\rho \le 0.09$), whereas format-level patterns replicate across runs. Two data families, worked examples and primitive facts, occupy $2.1$--$2.6\times$ their corpus share in both the helpful and harmful $5\%$ score tails, reflecting strong bidirectional local sensitivity distinct from net benefit under multi-epoch family deletion. These results show that trajectory attribution is reliable within short, validated windows and yields family-level insights that generalize across runs.

papers.title: The structure of varieties with nef anticanonical divisor in positive characteristic
Comparing Two-Sample IV Estimators under Weak Instruments
papers.abstract: We compare three estimators in a two-sample summary-data instrumental variables (IV) model: inverse-variance weighting (IVW), debiased inverse-variance weighting (dIVW), and the profile score (PS) estimator. The framework assumes independent samples and instrument-specific summary estimates, with two-sample Mendelian randomisation as a leading application. We compare existing fixed- and many-weak-instrument results and the sufficient conditions for the three estimators. Under the variance scaling used in the profile-score literature, the principal collective-strength conditions for PS and dIVW are equivalent, although their additional restrictions on instrument concentration and growth differ. We then compare their asymptotic variance formulae for fixed and diverging numbers of instruments. For fixed $L$, IVW and dIVW have the same first-order asymptotic variance. Under a common variance-ratio condition, the PS variance formula exceeds the IVW variance by a positive term of order $n^{-2}$, compared with the order-$n^{-1}$ leading variance. For diverging $L$, we establish variance orders across instrument-strength regimes and the exact ordering $\mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{IVW}} < V_{\mathtt{PS}} \leq \mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{dIVW}}$ under the same variance-ratio condition. Absolute variance gaps vanish when $\sqrt{L}\kappa\to\infty$, whereas relative equivalence holds if and only if $\kappa\to\infty$. These comparisons concern asymptotic variance formulae rather than finite-sample efficiency or mean squared error.

papers.title: A generic route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations
papers.abstract: We propose a generic autonomous route to chaos in self-excited plasma oscillations through nonlinear feedback from a finite-rate charging variable. Near the threshold of an oscillatory ion-acoustic instability, a multiple-scale reduction yields a Stuart-Landau amplitude equation, represented by a van der Pol-type modal surrogate and coupled to debris-charge evolution in a prototype case of plasma-debris interaction scenario. For a debris-induced ion-ion counter-streaming instability, charge-dependent forcing and frequency modulation, finite charging relaxation, phase-lagged modal response, mixed nonlinear feedback, and saturation form a closed dynamical system without an externally imposed periodic driver. Numerical bifurcation and Lyapunov analyses reveal multistability and a bounded chaotic branch reached through period doubling bifurcation and band formation. We test the proposed mechanism using a one-dimensional open-boundary \emph{hybrid} particle-in-cell-Monte Carlo collision simulation incorporating particle collection, photoemission, secondary-electron emission, and surface regulation. Weak-form sparse regression identifies finite intervals whose projected dynamics reproduce the sign structure of the reduced model, while independent $0$-$1$ chaos test, nonlinear predicatbility, surrogate-data, and Lyapunov diagnostics provide localized evidence of deterministic chaotic organization in the subsonic case. The combined results establish a proof-of-principle route by which a self-excited plasma mode can become chaotic through internally generated charging feedback.

papers.title: Physics-Grounded STL Monitoring from Image Observations
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation missions must satisfy timed and conditional requirements that can be expressed in signal temporal logic (STL). While a practical means of monitoring these requirements is from camera images, this is challenging because STL robustness depends on physical margins, such as distances and clearances, that are not directly observed. Rather than learning a separate visual monitor for each formula, we learn a shared latent representation from multi-view images and decode physically meaningful margins for individual predicates. Co-training the encoder with predicate decoders increases the certification rate from 58.7% to 96.3% compared with a frozen encoder, despite nearly unchanged predicate sign accuracy. STL semantics then compose these margins into robustness estimates for any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. We further calibrate the decoding errors of selected STL clauses using conformal prediction, yielding two-sided intervals that certify both satisfaction and violation and propagate through interval STL to any formula composed from the clauses. In simulated kitchen missions (LIBERO), our monitor correctly predicts satisfaction or violation in 98.9% of 4662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas. For missions lasting up to 17 min, calibrated bounds establish satisfaction or violation for 96.9% of missions without incorrect conclusions. A single calibration also provides simultaneous 91.0% coverage across all 255 conjunctions of eight clauses, allowing new formulas without recalibration.

papers.title: Adaptive Precision Cholesky with Error Guarantees
papers.abstract: Modern accelerators increasingly support low-precision formats such as 8-bit floats and integers to speed up machine learning. We show that a Cholesky factorization in which both GEMM and TRSM are implemented using the fixed-point Ozaki 1 scheme satisfies the same backward error bounds as the standard floating-point Cholesky factorization, and that the same holds for a Cholesky factorization computed using a low-precision MicroScaled GEMM. We then use our error analyses to construct an adaptive precision Cholesky factorization that exploits low-precision formats while respecting a prescribed element-wise error bound, as long as the factorization succeeds. We test it in two settings. First, we use it to choose the number of Ozaki 1 slices at each iteration, with SYRK/GEMM and TRSM emulated in INT8 fixed-point arithmetic to attain double-precision accuracy. Second, we use it to build a low-precision Cholesky preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method (PCG), in which SYRK/GEMM take low-precision inputs and accumulate in high precision, with the input format selected adaptively for each panel; if the factorization breaks down, diagonal perturbation still yields a valid preconditioner, at the cost of the error bound guarantees. On an NVIDIA GH200, the adaptive Ozaki 1-based factorization is up to 29% faster than a right-looking Cholesky using a fixed slice count of 7, and up to 69% faster than one using cuBLAS' Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP), while maintaining the same error guarantees. For PCG, FP8 factorizations with diagonal perturbation form effective preconditioners on the 13 tested SuiteSparse matrices, reducing the number of PCG iterations by up to $12\times$ over CG on the same matrix diagonally scaled by powers of two. For synthetic matrices with arithmetic spectra, and geometric spectra with $\kappa \le 10^4$, FP8 preconditioners also reduce the number of CG iterations.

papers.title: Elicited Adaptation: Auditable Localized Fairness via Pairwise Queries
papers.abstract: How much must a predictor's scores change when a community's elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. We study minimum uniform score movement on a fixed pool of $n$ profiles. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost $n-1$ times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the $n-1$ bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible $2$-approximate repair for tolerance $\eps\le1/[2(n-1)]$, reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in $n$. Feasible $(1+\alpha)$-optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity $\Theta(\alpha^{-2}n^2\log(1/\delta))$ under a fixed-slope logistic model. The analysis separates the information needed for a substantial adaptation benefit from the precision needed for nearly optimal movement. Elicitation studies and training comparisons examine tolerance choice and the relation between numerical compliance and predictive utility.

papers.title: A Five-Dimensional Geometric Formulation of Geophysical Fluid Dynamics
Early Readability of Trajectory Quality in Diffusion Driving Planners
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based driving planners can generate multiple trajectories for the same scene, but these candidates vary in quality. Can their internal states reveal which candidate will be better before denoising is complete? We systematically study this question in three pretrained planners: Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, using linear probes to predict final trajectory quality from intermediate states and evaluating candidate ranking and selection on held-out scenes. Across all three planners, we observe that states from the first denoiser evaluation already support informative selection, while further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality. Further analyses show that readout depends on the representation and reader, and that selection can coexist with limited overall ranking accuracy. These findings motivate an early-selection method that selects after the first denoiser evaluation and completes only the chosen candidate. This reduces computation relative to fully denoising every candidate and improves open-loop trajectory quality over random selection across all three planners. In particular, it reduces Alpamayo's average displacement error by 17.8% and 13.4% in one- and four-camera configurations, respectively. Closed-loop evaluations also show higher mean driving scores and progress.

papers.title: Inequality-Constrained Optimization via Sliding Mode Control
papers.abstract: We present COSMIC (Constrained Optimization via Sliding Mode for Inequality Constraints), a continuous-time solver for inequality-constrained optimization. COSMIC couples primal gradient-flow dynamics with multiplier dynamics derived from sliding mode control laws on a manifold defined by the smoothed Fischer-Burmeister function. We prove that COSMIC's trajectories reach this manifold in finite time from any primal initial point, after which the dynamics reduces to the gradient flow of a logarithmic barrier function. This yields a control-theoretic interpretation of barrier methods while allowing infeasible initialization. For strongly convex problems, we further establish exponential convergence to the minimizer. To address the numerical stiffness that arises in discretization, we develop a modified discrete-time algorithm. We validate COSMIC across various machine learning applications, demonstrating its ability to solve optimization problems accurately while scaling effectively to high-dimensional settings.

papers.title: Dymnikova black string
papers.abstract: We obtain a new static black string solution of Einstein's equations with a negative cosmological constant sourced by a Dymnikova-type anisotropic matter distribution. At large radial distances, the geometry approaches the Lemos black string, while the behavior near the central region is characterized by an effective curvature parameter. We examine the weak and strong energy conditions, the horizon structure, and the curvature invariants. The Ricci and Kretschmann scalars remain finite at the origin. We also investigate the Hawking temperature and heat capacity, with particular attention to the dependence of the thermodynamic behavior on the Dymnikova scale.

papers.title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
papers.abstract: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.

papers.title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

papers.title: A discontinuous time to collision feedback: well posedness, regularity of the collision-time map, and residual stability of its Hamilton Jacobi approximations
$\ell^p$-Busemann space and the coarse Novikov conjecture
Maximal dissipativity for the Dirichlet operator associated to the dynamical $Φ^4$ model on the plane
Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
papers.abstract: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

papers.title: Equivariant homomorphisms and Mordell--Weil groups of twists of Albanese varieties of cyclic multiple planes
Entanglement and Charge Transfer
papers.abstract: We compute the entropic order parameter introduced in ( 1905.10487 ) using the replica trick for two disjoint intervals. For a global symmetry, this quantity measures the mutual information carried by charge-anticharge intertwiners. We formulate the problem in terms of averages over twisted partition functions on replica Riemann surfaces, and obtain exact solutions for free fermions and compact bosons, for $U(1)$ symmetry and its discrete $\mathbb Z_N$ subgroups. We show that further averaging over both families of non-contractible cycles gives access to an additional quantity, which is the loss of Holevo information associated with complementary-charge measurements that occurs upon removing the intertwiners. For the boson, this quantity vanishes, whereas for Dirac fermions it equals the difference between the mutual information of the fermion-parity-gauged and ungauged theories, independently of the choice of even $\mathbb Z_N$ subgroup. Finally, we extend the analysis to non-Abelian symmetries using saddle expansions, deriving universal behavior in the nearly touching intervals limit and for a large number of fermions $N_F\gg1$.

papers.title: Bi-Lipschitz right-left equivalence of finite plane-to-plane germs
Wobbling Motion in the Many-Nucleon System
papers.abstract: The purpose of this Perspective is not to present a new progress but to shed light on another stream of the study of the nuclear wobbling motion from a viewpoint of the many-body theory under an external field. Special attention is paid to the moments of inertia, which are microscopically calculated as a response of the full $A$-body system to rapid rotations described by the cranked RPA formalism. They depend on the rotation frequency, and it is shown that approach of two moments of inertia leads to the instability of rotating triaxial mean fields.

papers.title: Shallow Clifford circuits on square lattices
papers.abstract: We study the depth of CZ circuits, Clifford state preparation, and Clifford unitary synthesis over the two-dimensional square lattice. A programmable circuit on a $2{\times}k$ ladder ($n{=}2k$) implements an arbitrary CZ computation in depth at most $\frac{3n}{2}{+}3$ up to reversal of both rails. This improves the best-known LNN (Linear Nearest-Neighbor)-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ construction by about 25\%. For state preparation, we consider a Phase gate programmable -H-{CNOT+P}-LC- circuit and derive matching obstructions to attaining the CZ-span counting lower bound of $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ for depth by the entangling gates. For cycle connectivity $C_n$, we prove that the minimum depth is exactly $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ when $n$ is not a multiple of four and $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ when $n\,{=}\,4k$. We construct a hole-free minimum-perimeter square-lattice patch with a Hamiltonian cycle for every even size, giving optimal-depth programmable circuits to implement Clifford states for all $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$. Exhaustive and heuristic searches address the remaining cases for $n$ up to 256, and selected values up to 1,024 qubits. The improvement against comparable state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ solution, is about 50\%. Finally, combining state synthesis circuits developed in this work with a known four-diagonal-stage decomposition gives rise to a depth $4n{-}4$ for $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$ and depth $4n$ for $n\,{=}\,4k$ implementation of arbitrary Clifford unitaries. This improves the most relevant state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth $7n{-}4$ construction, by about 43\%.

papers.title: Architecting the Corporate AI Infrastructure: The Evolving Roles of AI Governance Committees and Chief Ethics Officers
papers.abstract: The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into core business operations has created an urgent need for robust corporate governance infrastructures capable of managing complex ethical, legal, and operational risks. While organizations have increasingly adopted high-level AI ethics principles, a critical implementation gap persists: fewer than half of organizations that cite AI governance as a boardroom priority have a formalized governance framework in place. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a structured corporate AI governance architecture (CAIGA) centred on two mutually reinforcing pillars. First, it examines the evolving mandate of specialized C-suite roles, specifically Chief Privacy Officers (CPOs) and Chief Ethics Officers (ChEOs), in formalizing accountability for AI usage across the enterprise. Second, it argues that cross-functional AI Governance Committees, uniting representatives from legal, technology, data science, cybersecurity, and business units, are the essential organizational mechanism for translating ethical principles into operational decisions, including strategic go/no-go approvals for new AI initiatives. Drawing on a conceptual review of peer-reviewed governance literature, regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act, and documented industry practice, this paper contributes a replicable governance architecture that embeds clear accountability policies, structured risk management workflows, and an organization-wide ethical AI culture. The framework is illustrated through application to the financial services sector. The findings have direct implications for corporate leaders, risk professionals, and policymakers navigating the rapidly evolving global AI regulatory landscape.

papers.title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
papers.abstract: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

papers.title: Enumerating Solutions to Type (2,3) Composition Identities of Finite Endofunctions
Low-Voltage Ride-Through in AI Data Centers via Coordinated Battery and Computing Load Control
papers.abstract: The ability of large AI data centers to ride through grid voltage sags is critical to power system stability and reliability. This paper frames data center low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) as a DC-link power balance problem. Once the rectifier reaches its current limit, the power drawn from the grid decreases in proportion to the grid voltage. The DC-link capacitor can supply the resulting power deficit only briefly before the DC-link voltage falls low enough to trigger undervoltage protection tripping. To address this issue, this paper proposes effective control strategies for coordinating uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery and computing load curtailment to offset the power deficit and enable LVRT at minimum control cost. Three control scenarios are studied: UPS battery support alone, computing load curtailment alone, and the coordinated use of both resources. Electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations using the TAMU-ERCOT AI data center model demonstrate that battery support and the coordinated strategy achieve LVRT for all tested sags, including a near-zero-voltage fault, while load curtailment alone rides through moderate voltage sags.

papers.title: Lau's Fixed Point Problem for Elementary Amenable Groups and Finite Left Amenable Semigroups
Real zeros of Durfee polynomials: Proof of the Canfield--Corteel--Savage conjecture
Spectral coincidence and generalized Hua inversion in rings and Banach algebras
When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
papers.abstract: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

papers.title: Identifying Time Preference Shocks: Stated and Revealed Preferences after an Italian Earthquake
papers.abstract: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference. Jointly examining stated and revealed preferences resolves this identification problem: impatience shocks and reductions in financial resources generate opposite consumption responses, even though both raise stated impatience. Applying our identification framework to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, we combine panel data with spatially granular seismic and damage data in a difference-in-differences design that compares undamaged households that experienced the earthquake with a spatial control group at similar distances from the epicenter. Treated households report greater impatience and increase nondurable consumption by 11 percent relative to controls. Effects are consistent with a psychological stress channel, concentrated among the most vulnerable to stress, and persist as households deplete their liquid wealth buffer over time.

papers.title: Minimal time of null-controllability of the multi-dimensional singular Grushin equation
PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
papers.abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $\epsilon$-stationary control in $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $\epsilon$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/\epsilon$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.

papers.title: Associahedra are 8-colourable
papers.abstract: Determining the chromatic number of associahedra is a long-standing open problem. Tan [ arXiv:2611.05323 ] recently proved that associahedra are 12-colourable, which is the first constant upper bound. This paper adapts Tan's argument to show that associahedra are 8-colourable.

papers.title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

papers.title: Kepler as an accidental heliospheric imager: Thomson-scattered solar-wind structure in four years of background photometry
papers.abstract: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 May to 2013 May while staring at a fixed 12-degree field at ecliptic latitude +65 degrees. From this archive we isolate a large-scale layer that measures brightness variations relative to an 8-day running median. This layer contains fluctuations of 0.02-0.1 electrons per second per pixel (about 1e-17 of the mean solar surface brightness) that sweep across the field in a day or less. Four lines of evidence show that these are sunlight Thomson-scattered by solar-wind electrons. (1) The sweeps propagate away from the Sun (84 percent within 45 degrees of the anti-solar direction; 25 percent expected by chance), and their direction follows the Sun through each quarter and across all 16 spacecraft rolls. (2) The field brightness correlates with the near-Earth (OMNI) proton density within a day of zero lag (r = 0.19, p < 1/150), but not with the energetic-proton flux. (3) Time-elongation maps show fronts moving outward at a median 15 degrees per day, as forward models of radially moving density structures predict. (4) The amplitude is about one third of a parameter-free Thomson-scattering prediction and varies by a factor of about 3 over the year, as predicted. Half of the scattered light comes from within 0.4-0.7 AU of the spacecraft. Fronts are strongest in slow wind. Kepler's background pixels thus provide a four-year, high-cadence, out-of-ecliptic record of solar-wind structure near 1 AU. Standard Kepler processing removes these signals, changing stellar light curves by less than about 1 ppm.

papers.title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

papers.title: User First Intelligence: Three Measurements of Search and AI-Answer Analytics (SEO and GEO/AEO), and a Knowledge-Graph Framework for Query Discovery Beyond Search Volume
papers.abstract: People say what they want to know in many places besides a search box, and the tools that search and AI-answer optimization (SEO and GEO/AEO) rely on see only part of that demand, through models reported as counts. This paper reports three measurements of such instruments and a framework. On the area-code section of a large US telecom provider's site, two commercial analytics platforms differed on estimated monthly visits by 7.5x to 27.1x (8.6x to 29.9x worldwide); across twelve sections of the domain the ratio ran from 0.20x to 7.24x with no detectable relation to section age, while they agreed on which section is larger in 60 of 66 pairs. On 37,193 reviews of 378 telecom stores linked to a 42,994-node keyword taxonomy, review demand and search volume agreed on branches to a varying degree (Spearman 0.47 to 0.75; 0.91 post hoc) and barely on topics (0.18), on links two blind AI annotators judged two-thirds correct; on the 372 area codes, a public count of Wikipedia requests for each code and vendor volume agreed roughly on ranking (0.45 over 240 articles, gone once keywords matched per code are held constant) and not on magnitudes, predictions fixed first. In one vendor's index of AI answers naming or citing the largest companies of each S&P 500 sector, of four predictions written first, one held, one in direction only and two failed; video and community sites took a median 21% of citation incidences on Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode against 0.6% to 9.2% on four other surfaces, in every sector, and in education answers in each of 13 countries read later. Estimates and sources need measuring per instrument and surface. User First Intelligence (UFI), built on that premise, collects what people ask beyond the website, links it to an industry ontology and scores where an organization does not answer; an open implementation is released, its score not evaluated. No causal claim is made.

papers.title: Electromagnetic cross section of charmonium decay
papers.abstract: As an important measurable quantity, the electromagnetic cross sections of charmonium decay in an e+e- collider are valuated for fifteen final states. A general scheme of lS-coupling analysis is adopted for constructing covariant helicity-coupling amplitudes involving two-body decays with arbitrary integer spins. Based on the decay rate, the collision cross section is obtained finally. A number of illustrative examples is worked out to expound and incarnate the general formulas.

papers.title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
papers.abstract: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $d\sigma^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $\sigma^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

papers.title: LLM Facilitation of Group Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

papers.title: Quadrupole Origin of the Orbital Hall Effect in an $sp^3$ Centrosymmetric Lattice: Robustness and Tunability under Disorder
papers.abstract: We investigate how disorder affects orbital Hall transport in the centrosymmetric spinless $sp^3$ tight-binding model on a square lattice, widely used as a minimal model for the orbital Hall effect [1]. In the pristine system, the intrinsic orbital Hall response is related to the quadrupolar orbital texture generated by $s$-$p$ hybridization. Using the Kubo-Bastin formalism expanded in Chebyshev polynomials, we analyze the effect of vacancies, orbital-dependent Anderson on-site disorder, and selective $V_{sp\sigma}$-bond disorder on the orbital transport. For Anderson disorder and vacancies, the longitudinal charge conductivity decreases faster than the orbital Hall conductivity over the range studied, leading to an increase of the orbital Hall angle and, in the Anderson case, saturation at stronger disorder. Selective $V_{sp\sigma}$-bond disorder behaves differently: by modifying only the $s$-$p$ hybridization channel while leaving the remaining hopping network intact, it can produce a non-monotonic orbital Hall response and enhance the orbital Hall conductivity at intermediate dilution. Overall, our results show that the orbital Hall response remains sizable under vacancy and on-site disorder, while selective modification of the $s$-$p$ hybridization provides an additional route to tune the orbital Hall conductivity.

papers.title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
papers.abstract: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

papers.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

papers.title: High-energy asymptotics for the spectral actions of free particles in thermal equilibrium
Invariance of Arens module actions on the norm dual of a Riesz-normed f-algebra
A Numerical Approach to Quantization
papers.abstract: We introduce a numerical approach that simultaneously searches for matrix quantizations and compatible Poisson structures on classical geometric surfaces. Our method identifies irreducible Hermitian matrix representations and a trainable Poisson multiplier by minimizing a loss function that penalizes violations of the Casimir and commutation constraints. Through numerical investigations and subsequent theoretical analysis, we establish a no-go theorem showing that, for Weyl quantized fuzzy spheres with nondegenerate axial spectrum, the matrix dimension cannot exceed the degree of the nonconstant polynomial axial Poisson multiplier. We further extend our approach to nonpolynomial Poisson multipliers, demonstrating its versatility and potential to drive novel discoveries. Although here we focus on Weyl quantized fuzzy spheres, the framework is extensible to general geometric manifolds and quantization schemes. Our approach also provides a practical starting point for investigating Schild string theory and the quantization of spacetime histories.

papers.title: Formulation of Brownian chain molecular dynamics and the path-resolved quasi-density operator
papers.abstract: Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD) [M. Shiga, J. Comput. Chem. 43, 1864 (2022)] was introduced as a practical path-integral-based approach to approximate quantum vibrational dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems. Its equations of motion combine Newtonian dynamics of the centroid variables with overdamped Brownian dynamics of the non-centroid path variables. Here, we introduce a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation by extending the QDO construction underlying centroid molecular dynamics to the full discretized imaginary-time path. For two position-diagonal observables, this representation gives an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function in the fine-discretization limit, without requiring either observable to be linear. BCMD can be viewed as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced propagation in these path variables, although its generator is not derived from the path-QDO formulation. We also formulate and validate a multiple-time-step algorithm that allows pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in the deterministic propagation to be controlled by separating the Brownian refresh interval from the inner integration time step. We test the path-QDO representation on one-dimensional models and present BCMD infrared spectra of q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water, comparing them with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.

papers.title: Is Gravity a Real Force or Merely a Geometrical Effect?
papers.abstract: Whether gravitation should be regarded as a fundamental force or as a manifestation of spacetime geometry remains an interesting conceptual question in physics. In Newtonian mechanics, gravitation is described as a force acting between massive objects, whereas General Relativity describes gravitational phenomena in terms of spacetime curvature, with freely falling bodies following geodesics. With this fundamental difference, it is legitimate to ask whether gravity is a real force or not, and it is very common to receive from experts a somewhat condescending answer such as "Drop a rock on your foot and you will feel that the force is real". This paper does not attempt to determine whether gravity is fundamentally a force or a geometrical phenomenon. Rather, it questions whether commonly invoked everyday experiences provide valid grounds for deciding between these interpretations.

papers.title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
papers.abstract: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.
