This study develops a comprehensive Bayesian stochastic calibration framework integrating sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation via a Metropolis-Hastings within Gibbs sampling scheme with a novel Bias-Variance Cone analysis for asymptotic parameter identification. The framework is applied to 17 macroscopic speed-density models using one full year of 5-minute PeMS loop detector data from three California freeway stations. Sequential MCMC progressively increases the number of randomly sampled days from 1 to 365, enabling systematic evaluation of parameter stability and convergence as a function of data availability. Among the 17 models, nine achieved stable posterior convergence with physically interpretable estimates, while four exhibited catastrophic structural failures due to logarithmic singularities, unit incompatibilities, and initialization sensitivity. The Bias-Variance Cone framework, representing the first application of asymptotic bias-variance decomposition to fundamental diagram calibration, establishes that free-flow speed parameters are reliably identified within approximately 30 days, whereas density and shape parameters require 100 to 182 days, providing the first quantitative minimum data requirements in the literature. Collectively, the findings provide an empirical identifiability ranking of 17 fundamental diagram models, a validated minimum data sufficiency framework, and a replicable, automated platform for large-scale stochastic fundamental diagram calibration.

papers.title: Puzzle: One Pass Is Not Enough for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary remote sensing image segmentation (OVRSIS) enables the segmentation of unseen classes without additional annotation or retraining. By analyzing the predictions of existing OVRSIS methods, we find that many misclassified patches coexist with visually similar, correctly classified patches of the same class within the same image. Unfortunately, most of these methods stop after a single inference rather than using their predictions to guide further inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Puzzle}, a plug-and-play iterative re-inference framework that combines prediction history with a visual-similarity prior to progressively refine patch-level attention. Puzzle employs a lightweight history-conditioned controller to regulate each patch's contribution as an information source and its reliance on visually similar patches, while an adaptive stopping rule determines when to stop. It keeps the segmentation model frozen and reuses the same controller across different models and datasets without retraining. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements across diverse OVRSIS models and datasets, highlighting the strong transferability of Puzzle. Moreover, Puzzle can further improve the performance of SOTA methods.

papers.title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.

papers.title: Large-$N$ expansion in SU($N$) Yang-Mills-like theories
papers.abstract: It has been known for fifty years that bare U($N$) pure Yang-Mills (YM) theory admits the large-$N$ 't Hooft expansion for the $n$-point connected correlators of gauge-invariant single-trace operators, where the corresponding Feynman diagrams are topologically classified by the sum over the genus $g$ of $n$-punctured smooth orientable closed Riemann surfaces. In fact, 't Hooft expansion extends verbatim to U($N$) YM-like theories whose Lagrangians only involve fields valued in the U($N$) Lie algebra - including supersymmetric (SUSY) extensions of pure YM theory such as $\mathcal{N}=1,4$ SUSY YM. The aim of the present paper is to systematically work out the topology of the large-$N$ expansion in SU($N$) - as opposed to U($N$) - YM-like theories, where a number of subtleties inevitably arise. Indeed, since the U($1$) inside the U($N$) YM-like theories decouples, the large-$N$ U($N$) and SU($N$) expansions should either essentially coincide or intrinsically differ - in the latter case necessarily by extra - possibly singular - topologies, as the 't Hooft expansion in U($N$) YM-like theories already exhausts all the smooth topologies. In fact, we demonstrate that 't Hooft smooth topologies are actually generically incomplete in the large-$N$ expansion of both the SU($N$) and renormalized U($N$) YM-like theories, where renormalization inevitably separates the SU($N$) sector that is interacting from the U($1$) sector that is free. Specifically, we interpret the extra topologies that arise in SU($N$) theories for correlators of higher-twist quasi-partonic operators as singular pinched closed surfaces, thus extending our previous investigation of correlators of twist-$2$ operators for which extra pinched tori arise.

papers.title: Live Noise Fingerprints for Quantum Program Analysis
papers.abstract: Quantum programs are probabilistic in nature, and noisy execution due to current imperfect hardware further complicates their analysis. In this paper, we study abstract semantics for analysing quantum programs under these conditions. We introduce noise fingerprints, compact descriptions of the observable effects of noise relative to a finite interface of input states and output measurements. We use them to define our abstract domain with respect to the concrete noise-related behaviour. We relate the concrete and abstract domains through a probabilistic Galois connection, extending the Galois-connection framework to distribution-valued interpretations. We study the resulting abstraction in terms of observational soundness, conciseness, efficiency, and ability to adapt to changing noise. We show that polynomial-size interfaces yield exponentially smaller fingerprints than full noise models while preserving the chosen observations, and that fingerprint distance characterises the largest observational discrepancy over the chosen interface. Further, we develop ChanShadow, which reuses noise fingerprints of commonly used short program fragments to analyse noisy execution of whole programs and provides a uniform finite-sample error bound. We construct working examples showing how fingerprints support program analysis. We evaluate fingerprint precision, representation cost, measurement requirements, and behaviour under noise drift. On a synthetic benchmark, fingerprints retain $(99 \pm 1)\%$ of the noise strength information of a full noise model. On simulated noise drift, reusing earlier measurements reduces the number of fresh measurement rounds needed to reach an error tolerance of $0.10$ by a factor of $2.3$ at $95\%$ confidence and by a factor of $27$ under the median-error criterion.

papers.title: Excitation-Selective Control of Protected Subradiant Antiresonances
Asymptotic efficiency of tests for quantum statistical models
When the Mythical Man-Month Meets Agentic Web Systems: Structured Coordination for Scalable Development
papers.abstract: As agentic systems are increasingly deployed to support complex Web tasks, multi-agent architectures offer greater parallelism, specialization, and task coverage. However, increasing the number of agents does not necessarily improve system performance, as communication, synchronization, redundant work, and coordination overhead may offset the benefits of additional agents. This presents a fundamental scaling challenge for agentic Web systems: how can agent populations be organized to balance task performance and coordination costs? To address this challenge, we systematically investigate the relationship between agent population size, per-agent token consumption, and coordination overhead in collaborative agentic systems. Experiments on complex Web-oriented software development tasks reveal a non-linear scaling pattern: per-agent token consumption initially decreases as the agent population grows, but eventually exhibits diminishing returns. Motivated by these findings, we introduce the Surgical Team Model (STM), a structured coordination framework that organizes agents through role specialization, constrained inter-agent communication, and coordinator-mediated task aggregation. Experiments on full-stack Web application development tasks show that STM achieves competitive task completion quality and comparable token consumption relative to representative baselines, while incurring higher execution latency.

papers.title: Spontaneous Chiral Superradiance of a Spin-1 Condensate in a Ring Cavity
papers.abstract: We investigate superradiant phase transitions in a spin-$1$ Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to a ring cavity, where two symmetry-related Raman processes couple the atomic spin states to counterpropagating cavity modes. Above the superradiant threshold, we find that the symmetry between the two Raman channels is spontaneously broken, giving rise to a chiral superradiant (CSR) phase. Despite the exchange symmetry of the Hamiltonian, the CSR state spontaneously selects one of the two propagation directions, with one cavity mode becoming macroscopically occupied while its counterpropagating partner remains dark. Spin-dependent collisions further reshape the superradiant phase diagram by selectively shifting the boundaries between the chiral and symmetric superradiant phases, a feature intrinsic to the multicomponent spin-$1$ manifold. For sufficiently negative spin-dependent interactions, the interaction-induced modification of the atomic level structure gives rise to a reversed plane-wave phase characterized by an inverted internal-state occupation. These results identify spontaneous selection between symmetry-related superradiant channels as a mechanism for generating chirality in many-body cavity QED and demonstrate how spin-dependent collisions control the resulting superradiant phase structure.

papers.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

papers.title: Intervals in affine Bruhat order
Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.

papers.title: How Much Determinism Can Fine-Tuning Buy? Margin Regularisation Against Batch-Induced Token Flips
papers.abstract: Greedy decoding at zero temperature is widely assumed to be deterministic, although the exact same prompt may yield different tokens depending on the number of other prompts sharing the batch for inference. The currently available solutions operate during inference, trading determinism for throughput. Can we train a model in such a way that fewer decoding steps would be susceptible? We characterize the perturbation empirically across six model families and three numerical precisions and observe two empirical facts about the measurement: the perturbation depends exactly on the representable precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32, in line with predictions based on mantissa bits) and the batch invariance happens accidentally at certain tensor shapes, allowing a practitioner to achieve zero nondeterminism merely by setting the sequence length. Then we apply hinge penalization of the model's top-1 / top-2 logit gap, scaled to twice the measured noise quantile. On GSM8K dataset it leads to a 35% reduction in token flips and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1%, at the cost of 1.3 - 2.9 accuracy points, increasing monotonically with the margin size. It does not affect the gap threshold sufficient for determinism: the logit gaps of surviving flips are unchanged (median 0.125 for all arms), as the hinge is a soft penalty and the largest hardware perturbation remains the same. We reject seven hypotheses, including a per-model viability diagnosis, holding on six models and falsified on the seventh.

papers.title: OGLE-2018-BLG-0829L: A Microlensing System with a Planet Orbiting a Star Possessing a Brown-Dwarf Companion
papers.abstract: We analyze the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0829, whose light curve exhibits a weak short-term anomaly in addition to the prominent caustic-crossing features of a binary lens. The anomaly cannot be explained by a binary-lens single-source (2L1S) model. We therefore investigate both binary-lens binary-source (2L2S) and triple-lens single-source (3L1S) interpretations and find that both models reproduce the additional anomaly, with the 3L1S model being favored by $\Delta\chi^2=15.1$. Under the favored 3L1S interpretation, the anomaly arises from a caustic induced by a planetary-mass companion, whereas the prominent caustic-crossing features are produced by the underlying binary lens. Combining the measured event timescale, $t_{\rm E}=7.55\pm0.30$ days, and angular Einstein radius, $\theta_{\rm E}=0.325 \pm 0.059$ mas, with a Bayesian analysis, we infer a lens system consisting of an M dwarf of mass $0.193^{+0.300}_{-0.098}\,M_\odot$, a possible brown-dwarf companion of mass $0.068^{+0.105}_{-0.034}\,M_\odot$, and a Saturn-mass planet of mass $0.337^{+0.522}_{-0.171}\,M_{\rm J}$. The companions have projected separations of approximately 3.6 au and 1.6 au from the primary, respectively. However, the physical interpretation remains tentative because potentially important higher-order effects have not been considered, and the dynamical stability of the proposed configuration remains uncertain. If confirmed, this would be the third star--brown dwarf--planet system identified through microlensing, highlighting the potential of microlensing to detect planets in complex multiple systems.

papers.title: Psyquandle Fares
The Race between Protection and Control: Fast Reactive Reserves Against Overvoltage Cascade
papers.abstract: In an overvoltage cascade, each relay trip removes reactive power absorption and raises the voltage at other plants, often faster than controls can act. This paper determines how much fast reactive power to hold, where, and how fast, so that no contingency trips a plant. A trip certificate allows a relay to pick up if it resets before its delay expires, making the sizing a linear program. A necessary condition identifies the relays that only preventive action can protect, and the reserve of one control decreases with the relay delay and increases with its latency. In nonlinear simulations of four systems, the corrective actions prevent every trip within the analysis window for relays without reset hysteresis, and each plant's own set point is the most effective reserve. A 2\% hysteresis or a small error in the relay voltage can change the reserve as much as the relay delay.

papers.title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.

papers.title: Accurate qLDPC decoding under real-time constraints
Classification of Conformal Ising/Tricritical Ising Interfaces Preserving $\mathcal{W}_3^{\mathbb{Z}_2}$ Symmetry
papers.abstract: We classify conformal interfaces between the Ising and tricritical Ising models that preserve the chiral algebra $\mathcal{W}_3^{\mathbb{Z}_2}$. Using the folding trick, we formulate the problem in terms of boundary states satisfying the Cardy condition and determine the unique NIM-rep compatible with the bulk partition function. We obtain a complete set of 24 fundamental boundary states, of which 18 correspond to factorized interfaces preserving the full product Virasoro symmetry, while the remaining six break this symmetry. We construct these six interfaces explicitly and determine their annulus partition functions. They are related by topological defect line dressings, and one coincides with the RG domain wall proposed by Gaiotto.

papers.title: Efficient simulation of the generalized Langevin equation using a basis of dynamically relevant histories for memory and noise
papers.abstract: The Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) is a cornerstone for modeling non-Markovian dynamics, but its numerical solution remains challenging due to the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function. We introduce a forward construction that addresses both challenges within a single framework. We represent an arbitrary trajectory as sum of relevant and irrelevant parts, where relevant part can be decomposed into a small number of characteristic history patterns that make the main contribution to future dynamics. It allows to reduce numerical cost to \(O(d^2)\) for $d$ chosen patterns instead of full history. The same construction applies to colored noise generation, where the causal filter plays the role of the memory kernel. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the method for several representative kernels, including long-range kernels with power-law tails.

papers.title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.

papers.title: A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.

papers.title: AI Inference-Aware Optimal Power Flow: Converting Token Requirements into Grid Flexibility
papers.abstract: The rapid growth, temporal variability, and geographic concentration of electricity demand from artificial intelligence (AI) inference can aggravate transmission congestion near data centers (DCs). The spatial and temporal flexibility of inference workloads offers an opportunity to alleviate this congestion: requests can be routed across DCs or deferred within users' quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. However, inference routing primarily considers graphics processing unit (GPU) availability, leaving this flexibility underused in grid operation. Using GPU measurements, this paper models inference latency and DC power consumption to quantify the flexibility available under users' time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) requirements. These models are then incorporated into an AI inference-aware optimal power flow (OPF) that coordinates inference routing and power system operation among DC operators, the transmission system operator, and inference users. By linking user requests, token generation at DCs, and electricity delivery through the transmission network, the formulation schedules inference workloads subject to both users' QoS requirements and transmission constraints. Simulations on the PJM system show that, compared with computing-based routing and with electricity price-based routing, coordinating inference routing with network operation enables growing DC electricity demand deliverable to be met at lower cost.

papers.title: ANCHOR: A Port-Hamiltonian Model for Forecasting Team Dynamics in Human-in-the-Loop Systems
papers.abstract: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On \nGroups{} four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.

papers.title: Beyond Plain MCP: Do Decision Models and Code Mode Make Tool Use Cheaper and Faster?
papers.abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateways manage tool catalogs for language model agents using two primary paradigms: code mode where agents write scripts against tool stubs and decision layers which are cheap routers that preselect tool subsets. Using a controlled harness across 12 servers, up to 1,958 distractor tools, and three open-weight agents including Qwen, Gemma, and Nemotron, we present a preregistered evaluation on a sealed test split to determine when each approach succeeds. Code mode substantially outperforms plain MCP, cutting token usage by 70 to 90 percent while significantly boosting utility. Declaring return-shape hints in code mode stubs is a first-order variable, swinging success by up to 39.5 points for lower-performing agents, an effect larger than adding a router. The central hypothesis that a decision layer in front of code mode beats code mode alone is not confirmed, showing minor, statistically non-significant improvements for weaker agents and a slight cost for the strongest. We publicly release our harness, a finetuned 4B tool selection model, and all evaluation traces to support robust community experimentation on local AI privacy and agent architectures.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Process Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
papers.abstract: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning, yet in complex multi-step reasoning, an error at any step may propagate along an incorrect path, and the resulting solution may omit necessary branches. Existing natural-language reflection methods often struggle to locate critical errors precisely, while outcome verification typically checks only whether the available candidate answers satisfy the problem conditions and can therefore overlook necessary branches. To address these limitations, we propose Agent-Guided Process Verification (AGPV) for mathematical self-correction. AGPV decomposes the current solution into an ordered sequence of key claims, verifies them individually while invoking a shared mathematical toolbox when needed, and stops upon detecting the first error. A summarization agent converts the failure evidence into a diagnosis that guides a correction agent to re-derive the subsequent solution from that point; AGPV then adapts the next verification iteration to the revised solution. AGPV also verifies solution completeness. We further prove that AGPV guarantees solution correctness and completeness when key claims provide sufficient coverage and local verification is reliable, provided that all key claims pass verification. The implementation compresses long working contexts and reuses successful tool results within each problem. We evaluate AGPV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with four models from DeepSeek, Qwen, and GPT. AGPV achieves an average accuracy of 63.8%, outperforming the strongest among the representative baselines evaluated (50.3%) by 13.5 percentage points, with higher repair coverage than the programmatic-verification baselines.

papers.title: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing
papers.abstract: While recent advances in multimodal image editing have achieved impressive results, current frameworks remain largely confined to ``flat" 2D controls (e.g., text prompts, bounding boxes, or masks). Precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation -- such as coordinating an object's location, physical scale, and 3D orientation while strictly preserving its fine-grained identity -- remains an elusive challenge, typically suffering from severe detail degradation or requiring expensive per-instance fine-tuning. In this paper, we present DecoEdit, an all-in-one image editing framework that goes beyond flat control by seamlessly integrating 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs under a unified architecture. First, to power this unified model, we establish a data curation pipeline and curate a large-scale dataset, namely DecoDataset, containing 1.6 million samples, encompassing diverse multi-dimensional (1D/2D/3D) tasks and their complex compositions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive image editing benchmark named DecoBench to systematically evaluate multi-task editing performance. Finally, to address the fundamental trade-off between complex spatial transformations and identity preservation, we propose a novel decoupled pipeline: DecoEdit factorizes the editing process by utilizing structural guidance from SAM-3D to anchor the target geometry, scale, and spatial orientation, while concurrently leveraging a detail-preservation path to lock in high-fidelity textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, on the challenging 3D spatial pose and orientation control tasks, DecoEdit significantly outperforms leading closed-source models such as Seedream 5.0 in both geometric accuracy and identity consistency.

papers.title: Joint RF-VLP Position and Velocity Tracking: Bayesian Estimation and Performance Analysis
papers.abstract: Visible light positioning (VLP) provides accurate indoor positioning through optical received signal strength (RSS) measurements, while radio-frequency (RF) delay and Doppler measurements offer complementary range and velocity information. Motivated by this complementarity, we investigate joint RF--VLP position and velocity tracking, addressing both recursive state estimation and its fundamental performance characteristics. We formulate a Bayesian maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problem that combines optical RSS, RF delay and Doppler measurements, and motion prediction, and develop a Gauss--Newton-based algorithm for recursive tracking. To characterize the estimation limits and the benefits of RF--VLP integration, we derive the Bayesian information matrix and the corresponding Bayesian Cramér--Rao lower bound (BCRLB). We further introduce a state-conditioned information matrix (SCIM), whose inverse coincides with the MAP estimator's mean-squared error matrix under a first-order observation model, enabling tractable analysis of RF-induced information gains. The analysis quantifies the distinct contributions of RF delay and Doppler measurements and reveals different asymptotic estimation-error behaviors with respect to RF and VLP signal-to-noise ratios. Numerical results demonstrate improved position and velocity tracking over the considered baselines, with substantial velocity gains from RF sensing. The results also validate the theoretical asymptotic predictions and show that the inverse of the SCIM closely captures the estimator's error trends.

papers.title: Pole rigidity in root-optimal rational approximation of the exponential on infinite sectors
papers.abstract: The optimal root convergence factor for uniform rational approximation of the exponential on an infinite sector is classical. We prove that, for every fixed infinite sector of opening less than $\pi$, the normalized pole-counting measures of any reduced root-optimal sequence, after scaling the poles by degree, converge weakly to a uniquely determined probability measure supported on a compact analytic arc outside the sector. For the half-line, the corresponding pole law was previously announced by Stahl and Schmelzer; our new result covers sectors of positive opening. The proof rules out boundary pole accumulation and controls an exponentially small Hermite residual through reflection and noncancellation, without assuming interpolation or orthogonality. We explicitly construct the equilibrium measure and its supporting arc in terms of a zero of a Ferrers function, and relate this parameterization to the Gonchar--Rakhmanov theta equation. We also obtain a degree-independent comparison for simultaneous approximation of finitely many $\varphi$-functions with a common denominator. Numerical pole distributions support the theoretical law.

papers.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
papers.abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

papers.title: Testing General Relativity by Reconstructing Dark Energy and the Growth Index with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We extend the Cosmo-PINN, a physics-informed neural network for model-independent cosmological reconstruction, to reconstruct the dark energy equation of state parameter $w_{\mathrm{DE}}(z)$ and the growth index $\gamma (z)$ of matter perturbations. The reconstruction is performed through three modules: the background module, the matter growth module, and the growth index module. The background module learns the dark energy density $\rho _{\mathrm{DE}}(z)$ from cosmological observations, and $w_{\mathrm{DE}}(z)$ is reconstructed through the residual of the conservation equation. The reconstructed background is then passed to the other two modules, which reconstruct the observables $f(z)$ and $f\sigma _{8}(z)$ either directly from the linear perturbation equation of General Relativity or through an independently reconstructed growth index $\gamma (z)$. Comparing the two reconstructions on the same background provides a consistency test of the underlying physical framework. The network is trained on the DESI DR2 Baryon Acoustic Oscillations, Cosmic Chronometers, Type Ia Supernovae, and redshift-space distortion data. Posterior uncertainties for the reconstructed cosmological parameters and functions are obtained through Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. For the different data combinations, the posterior median of the present-day dark energy equation of state lies within the range $w_{\mathrm{DE,0}}\in \lbrack -0.930,-0.867]$, while the phantom divide crossing takes place at $z\simeq 0.41$--$0.53$. The posterior median of the present-day growth index reconstructed from the data lies within $\gamma _{0}\simeq 0.60$--$0.62$, indicating suppression of the growth of cosmic structure.

papers.title: A Hybrid State Space-Attention Architecture for Forecasting the Trajectories of Battery Degradation
papers.abstract: Early-life battery degradation trajectory forecasting aims to predict a battery cell's full state-of-health (SOH) trajectory from its initial charge-discharge cycles, potentially reducing cell qualification and evaluation time from months to days. Despite recent advances, accurate forecasting remains challenging for emerging battery chemistries, data-scarce domains, and cells exhibiting degradation behaviors beyond those observed during training. Existing state-of-the-art approaches increasingly rely on model scaling, large language model-derived aging-condition embeddings, and extensive fold-specific hyperparameter tuning, raising concerns about computational efficiency, reproducibility, and generalization. This work introduces DecayFormer, a compact hybrid state-space and attention architecture designed for early-life degradation trajectory forecasting. DecayFormer combines cycle-level selective recurrence, using a single scalar state per channel, with an attention mechanism queried by the recurrent state. It further incorporates state-of-charge (SOC) interval statistics and a master curve head that jointly estimates a scalar lifetime and a monotonically non-increasing SOH profile parameterized by normalized lifetime. We evaluate DecayFormer on the BatteryLife benchmark using all 22 aging-condition-exclusive folds, with a single run per fold and one fixed configuration across all folds, without fold-specific tuning. DecayFormer achieves mean test MAPE values of 2.25% on Li-ion, 2.76% on CALB, 0.95% on Na-ion, and 7.19% on Zn-ion. These results demonstrate the potential of compact sequence models to deliver accurate early-life degradation forecasts across diverse battery chemistries and aging conditions, without relying on extensive model scaling or per-fold optimization.

papers.title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin predictive modeling across science, engineering and medicine. Their use in digital twins, parameter inference and optimal design requires repeated solutions across parameters and scenarios. For nonlinear, transient and multiphysics systems, these calculations can make numerical simulation prohibitively expensive. Here we introduce the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy using a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs and incorporates its correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction. We establish local error bounds for the residual-informed estimates under stability and smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate RI-BNO on a non-linear reaction-diffusion benchmark with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures, Markov chain Monte Carlo inference of glioma parameter fields from magnetic resonance imaging, and Monte Carlo risk-averse optimization of three-dimensional thermal breaks in building envelopes under manufacturing uncertainty. Across the evaluated examples, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element (FE) reference predictions, parameter posteriors and optimized designs while using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as the vanilla Bayesian neural operator (vBNO). For thermal break design, online optimization time decreases from 178 hours with the FE model to 18 minutes with RI-BNO. These results demonstrate the value of explicit inadequacy modeling in neural operators for reliable PDE-based inference and design.

papers.title: The Contact Process with Temporary Immunity on $\mathbb{Z}$
Decoupling Data Layouts from Algebraic Data Types
papers.abstract: Algebraic data types (ADTs) decouple the logical structure of data from physical layout choices that affect performance. For example, packing small fields into a word improves spatial locality, while storing co-accessed fields contiguously can enable vectorization. Such choices reinforce or undermine one another, with ramifications for compiler optimizations and memory management. Their interplay creates a combinatorial space of layouts with different runtime costs and memory footprints. The most favorable layout depends on the program's construction and destruction patterns, the characteristics of input data, and the target machine. Exploring this space requires control over layout decisions and a way to compose them while preserving program semantics. We provide both through rewrite rules over layouts, independent of any particular source language or bit-level encoding. Starting from a canonical layout derived from the ADT, these rules transform its representation while leaving the source program intact. We identify a local refinement criterion for proving each rewrite rule correct, so that layouts continue to represent every value and keep distinct values apart. Adding a new rule therefore only requires a proof satisfying this local criterion. We realize these rules in Isomer, a new pure functional programming language whose compiler specializes construction, pattern matching, and memory management to the chosen layouts. Using a default layout for all ADTs, Isomer achieves competitive performance against established functional compilers that automatically select layouts. Our rewrites further improve performance by tailoring layouts to each workload, permitting representations that prior work cannot attain or can only achieve through explicit changes to the source code.

papers.title: How to Agree Without Agreeing
papers.abstract: Consensus lets institutions decide without a central authority, but a record of agreement reveals neither its basis nor its credibility. We model support, standing aside and veto as responses to a proposal. A proposal can pass without active support, and the member least willing to allow passage limits what can be adopted, however many members oppose the proposal. Letting proposers moderate their demands can ease agreement while undermining the prescribed punishment. Proposal restrictions or deviation costs can preserve that threat. Across the initialisations tested, learning agents agree frequently even though many reconstructed rules allow profitable departures. In our sample of Antarctic Treaty working papers, 80% of proposals revising existing arrangements were adopted at submission, against 38% of new proposals. Consensus can keep producing agreement on what already exists while new protection waits.

papers.title: Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy
papers.abstract: Canada's 2026 national AI strategy, AI for All, commits to free AI training for everyone and to expanding business AI adoption, yet it is difficult to anticipate whether these policies will reach adults with uneven skills and circumstances. We ask how adults with diverse skills might rate these policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, how their skills and circumstances shape these evaluations, and what implementation conditions they raise. We built 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2 respondents, collected their ratings and explanations for 20 policies, and analyzed dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings. The agents supported nearly every policy but were far less confident that they would improve adult AI literacy or benefit them personally. This gap widened as digital technology use declined: agents modeled on adults who had never used a digital device still endorsed the policies but rarely expected to benefit. Agents traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control, and their dialogues specified these conditions rather than resolving disagreement. We describe this pattern as conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policy should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

papers.title: CLEAR: Legible and Steerable Recommendation via Grounded Natural-Language Interests
papers.abstract: Modern recommenders keep learned preferences in representations people cannot inspect or change. We present CLEAR (Controllable and Legible End-to-end Architecture for Recommendation), an end-to-end system deployed at Meta and built around an editable natural-language interest layer. CLEAR makes a ranked subset of inferred interests readable and stores accepted additions and suppressions as authoritative preference state. Behavioral grounding maps each inferred interest back to supporting events in the user's own history. The resulting interest object is also a serving address: its label and profile-conditioned rewrites drive lexical retrieval, its supporting events seed behavioral retrieval, its projection queries an embedding index, and its stable identity supports ranking, attribution, and exposure control. A fresh user declaration may precede behavioral support, so it enters through the same serving identity and initially draws candidates from topical retrieval. Ranking makes those candidates competitive, while a delivery controller observes attributable exposure and replenishes underexposed interests. Direct user review found that users rated about 88.5% of displayed interests accurate. In an offline benchmark using a shared evaluation protocol, the Specialized 3B generator reached 0.3967 mean-user F1@10, compared with 0.3633 for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 0.1911 for the prior generator. For a newly declared interest, a user-randomized cumulative ablation measured same-day delivery losses of 8.7 percentage points for added-interest ranking terms, 11.1 for reserved top-slot insertion, and 13.7 for interest-conditioned candidate sourcing, conditional on the tested removal sequence. CLEAR components have operated in production for over one year; the system spans four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook, with an interest layer people can inspect, correct, and use to direct recommendations.

papers.title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.

papers.title: Guiding AI Agents to Generate Conjectures by Encoding How Theorems Build on One Another
papers.abstract: Recently, LLMs have been making headlines, and headway, in mathematical research. Much of this work focuses on proving existing open conjectures. Deciding what to prove is harder and less studied, because of the lack of a clear criterion for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing. We present a method for conjecture generation that builds on the observation that mathematical theorems build on one another: new theorems can modify the setting or hypotheses of earlier theorems, strengthen their conclusions, or extend their scope. We encode these relationships in a new kind of graph, the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG), which we instantiate as an online search method for LLM agents. An agent builds a TEG in two steps: (1) identifying relevant theorems from papers found by following citations backward and forward from a seed paper; and (2) comparing those theorems to record how one builds on another. LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over those from an unconstrained baseline. LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight, and favored baseline conjectures for plausibility. Ablations suggest a benefit from constructing and using a TEG even when the available papers are fixed.

papers.title: NS-bialgebras, the NS-Yang-Baxter equation and dendriform D-bialgebras
Knowledge-Guided Local-to-Global Anomaly Learning for Longitudinal Medication Trajectories
papers.abstract: Detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories requires distinguishing knowledge-consistent treatment variations from anomalous changes and linking local deviations to account-level decisions. We propose a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework that addresses both challenges. It constructs proxy supervision at three granularities: medication occurrences, treatment episodes, and contiguous visit segments. Knowledge-consistent medication and episode replacements provide plausible negatives, while cross-category and cross-account perturbations provide suspicious proxies. A medication-multiset encoder and causal visit-sequence encoder feed a shared scoring head that produces visit-level anomaly logits. Top-\(\alpha\) aggregation derives account-level scores from these logits, while account-level classification and class-balanced visit-localization objectives jointly optimize the same visit-level evidence. Experiments on two city cohorts compare L2G with native and proxy-adapted anomaly methods. On City-A, L2G outperforms the strongest comparators. Cross-city results show more consistent gains in localization than in account-level detection.

papers.title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
papers.abstract: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

papers.title: EEGHyena2: Fixation-Inspired Joint Lexical-Grammatical Conditional Random Field for Interpretable EEG-to-Text Decoding
papers.abstract: A sentence is built from words that carry lexical meaning and grammatical roles, and brain activity during reading reflects both. Current EEG-to-text decoders, however, let a large language model (LLM) propose and order the words, so fluent output can reflect the LLM's prior more than the recorded EEG. In this study, we asked whether fixation-linked EEG carries lexical and grammatical evidence during natural reading and how a decoder can use such evidence. Fixation-related potential analyses showed that content and function words differ reliably in group-averaged EEG but only weakly in single words. We therefore propose EEGHyena2, a structured decoder in which a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeds a semantic head that ranks a fixed lexicon and a part-of-speech (POS) head that predicts grammatical categories; a joint word-POS conditional random field (CRF) scores a restricted candidate lattice, and a frozen Llama-2 scores the candidates in context. On two natural-reading corpora, ZuCo and ROAMM, it matched the state-of-the-art method on BLEU-1 (21.4 vs 21.3), exceeded it on ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs 20.3), lowered the character error rate on ROAMM (75.3% vs 84.7%) and decoded each recording about 3-10 times faster than LLM candidate search. The CRF learned transitions that mirror English syntax, and the encoder drew local context from its convolutions and distant context from attention. Decoders can thus pool weak word-level EEG evidence across the sentence through explicit lexical and grammatical structure, with the language model adjudicating among candidates rather than generating them, which lowers decoding cost and keeps decisions inspectable.

papers.title: The first-order theory of the ring of integers of any abelian extension of $\Q$ is undecidable
Stability of Self-Similar Expansions for Self-Gravitating Hyperelastic Bodies
A predictive, per-engine energy roofline of the Apple Neural Engine
papers.abstract: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.

papers.title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
papers.abstract: We study supported reaching to extend a humanoid robot's workspace by bracing against the environment for stabilization using a straightforward yet capable whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach, exclusively with local sensing and fiducial markers. While typical solutions for whole body humanoid control aim at avoiding or accommodating contact, contact is explicitly required to reach objects placed on surfaces far out of normal reach. We employ sampling-based MPC for whole-body leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The controller runs in real-time at 34 Hz on a laptop, transfers sim-to-real, extends reach by about 50 cm beyond the unbraced standing workspace, and sustains the loaded posture for over four minutes, before pose estimation drifts. The controller reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, across 54 trials spanning six targets and three table heights. We further characterize why such a small real-time sampling budget is sufficient, finding that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale strongly govern success, while CEM provides the widest operating region over planning rate and model mismatch. These results establish a real-world baseline for online, contact-rich humanoid manipulation. Code, videos, and full hardware details are available at this https URL

papers.title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
papers.abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

papers.title: Drift of a Charged Particle in a Black Hole Magnetosphere: the Effect of Black Hole Spin
papers.abstract: Sparse plasma immersed in a strong magnetic field is common in astrophysical scenarios, for which a collisionless description is more appropriate. The guiding-center approximation serves as an effective tool for describing the motion of charged particles in a strong magnetic field, revealing the drift, a sub-leading order motion that causes particles to deviate from the magnetic field lines. It is widely accepted that the charged particles drift under the induction of gravity in Newtonian framework. However, a covariant formulation of the guiding-center approximation, as well as the drift of a charged particle induced by strong gravitational field, has yet to be fully explored. As a preliminary study, we aim to analyze the drift of a single charged particle in a black hole magnetosphere via a covariant approach. Particularly, we focus on the effects of black hole spin. We first examine the drift caused by the rotation of a massive object in the Newtonian regime using the language of gravitoelectromagnetism. A covariant formula of drift is derived, which is confirmed to reduce to the Newtonian results in the weak gravitational field and low speed limit. The impact of BH spin on the drift is analyzed in detail in Kerr spacetime specifically, for which we define the drift rate whose value quantifies the significance of the drift. Our results indicate that the impact of BH spin on the drift of a charged particle in a BH magnetosphere can be comparable to that of other factors in some extreme cases.

papers.title: Conditional Principle of Least Action: Gauge Algebra and Noether's Second Theorem
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of a conditional extremum of an action within a class of fields constrained by differential equations. For this setup, we establish the interconnection between the gauge symmetry algebra of the equations constraining the admissible fields and that of the action restricted to this class of fields. Based on this relation between the two gauge algebras, we derive an extension of Noether's second theorem and its converse. The general method is illustrated by the example of linearized gravity with the Einstein-Hilbert action and the class of admissible metrics restricted by the Cotton equation.

papers.title: AdaptType: Accessible and Customizable Multimodal Text Entry in Virtual Reality for People with Upper-Body Motor Impairments
papers.abstract: Text entry in virtual reality (VR) is cumbersome, especially for people with upper-body motor impairments. Existing techniques often demand both fine and gross motor control, yet users' motor abilities vary widely. To address this range of needs, we present AdaptType, a multimodal VR text entry system that enables users to configure input techniques that best suit their abilities, and scaffolds customization through ability-based recommendations. Through a study with 10 participants, we found that customized multimodal techniques improved text entry speed compared to gaze- or hand-only techniques, and complemented voice for error correction, decreasing failure rate from 15.1% to 2.0%. We found that AdaptType yielded high text entry speed (36.26 WPM) and accuracy (0.36% error rate), with low task load and high usability ratings. We also found ability-based recommendations effectively scaffolded customization. Our work contributes more accessible and personalized VR text entry solutions for people with upper-body motor impairments.

papers.title: DEFDVO: Deformable Deep Visual Odometry for Equirectangular Images
papers.abstract: Omnidirectional ($360^\circ$) cameras capture the full surrounding scene in every frame, providing a strong advantage for visual odometry (VO) over pinhole sensors with a limited field of view. However, their equirectangular projection (ERP) introduces latitude-dependent distortion, an artificial seam at the image border, and a sampling bias toward the poles. Existing $360^\circ$ VO methods address these challenges only partially. DEFDVO closes this gap with a patch-based deep VO method that operates directly on ERP imagery, combining spherically initialized deformable feature extraction, end-to-end seam-aware estimation, and spherical-gradient patch selection. The deformable feature extractor combines spherical geometric priors with learned sampling offsets, while seam-aware processing preserves ERP continuity, and spherical-gradient selection reduces polar sampling bias. Trained exclusively on synthetic TartanAirV2 ERP imagery, DEFDVO improves the best prior average absolute trajectory error (ATE) by $4.8\times$ (0.201 m to 0.042 m) on the TartanAirV2 evaluation set defined by 360DVO and achieves the lowest average ATE on both splits of the real-world 360DVO benchmark. Code is available at this https URL

papers.title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
papers.abstract: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.

papers.title: ASASSN-15af: An Eclipsing Cataclysmic Variable above the Period Gap Showing Both Positive and Negative Superhump-like Signals
papers.abstract: We present a photometric study of ASASSN-15af (TIC~231050794), combining TESS full-frame-image photometry from the TEQUILA project with 2-minute SPOC light curves and archival ASAS-SN and ATLAS monitoring over 4400~d. The long-term light curve shows recurrent dwarf-nova outbursts, establishing ASASSN-15af as a high-inclination eclipsing dwarf nova above the canonical period gap. From 391 quiescent eclipses, we derive the working ephemeris $T(E)=2139.76108(3)+0.14982063(2)\,E$ (BTJD), corresponding to $P_{\rm orb}=3.596$~hr. A quadratic fit is formally better, but the timings sample only three widely separated epochs, so we regard the apparent O--C curvature as tentative. In quiescence, the out-of-eclipse waveform is dominated by a stable $2f_{\rm orb}$ component, consistent with a substantial ellipsoidal contribution from the donor; during the Sector~96 outburst, its fractional amplitude decreases by $\simeq66\%$, consistent with dilution by the brightened disk. The outburst-only signals occur at periods $\sim1.6\%$ shorter than $P_{\rm orb}$ in Sector~2 and $\sim3.1\%$ longer in Sector~96, consistent with negative- and positive-superhump-like modulations, respectively. Because each is detected in only one outburst, their recurrence remains to be established. Their period-offset ratio, $\phi\simeq0.51$, is consistent with empirical trends among systems showing both modes, while the inferred superhump-based mass ratios span $q\simeq0.06$--$0.24$. During the Sector~96 outburst, the eclipse deepens by $\Delta D=0.196\pm0.028$ and its centroid shifts earlier by $\Delta t_{\rm c}=-66.6\pm7.3$~s, indicating a redistribution of accretion-powered light. These results identify ASASSN-15af as an above-gap eclipsing dwarf nova with a dynamically variable accretion disk; spectroscopy is needed to constrain the mass ratio.

papers.title: Constrained Adiabatic Quantum Programming
On the Flucher--Rumpf isoperimetric question for the interior Bernoulli free boundary problem: a conformal reformulation, quantitative bounds and the second variation at the disc
When the Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks on LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become used more commonly across a variety of fields, a growing body of research has highlighted particular concerns surrounding model security. Notably, prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into prompts, are particularly simple to implement yet capable of inducing devastating effects on the fidelity of model outputs. While there is substantial research surrounding attack models and their effects on chat-based models, browser add-ons, and coding agents, the impact of these same attacks on industrial LLM-generated artifacts has been left largely unexplored. As LLM-enabled agents are increasingly used to skim and generate industrial documents such as Safety Data Sheets (SDS), Quality Control (QC) documents, and Digital Product Passports (DPP), it remains unclear how adversaries may influence these systems to manipulate generated compliance artifacts. This work aims to address this core inquiry by examining how a variety of prompt injection attacks can compromise LLMs with industrial document generation tasks. The study finds that injection attack success varies significantly across different models. Active falsification injections are most successful under all scenarios, while models tend to be most robust against passively injected override requests.

papers.title: FDAM: A Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Pavement Crack Grid Localization
papers.abstract: Pavement crack grid localization remains challenging for thin and tiny cracks due to weak visual cues and background interference. Box detection often misses these cracks, while supervised semantic segmentation faces limited pixel-wise annotations and high labeling costs. In this paper, we propose a Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task framework (FDAM) with box detection and grid classification branches. The core grid classification branch comprises Frequency-Domain Enhancement (FDE) and Directional Feature Refinement (DFR). FDE adaptively weights spectral bands and fuses reconstructed features with spatial features. DFR captures thin crack patterns through multi-scale strip convolutions, direction-sensitive modulation, and feature recalibration. Sparse positive cells and ambiguous local predictions motivate adaptive grid supervision. Adaptive Importance Reweighting emphasizes uncertain predictions and local label transitions, with focal supervision for all cells. Our contribution is to couple the box detection and grid classification branches through shared feature learning for pavement crack grid localization. We validate FDAM on our RoadDistress2026 dataset of thin and tiny cracks and further evaluate it on public datasets Crack500 and DeepCrack. The code is available at this https URL

papers.title: Reliable Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability via Subsolution Learning on Exact Local Windows
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.

papers.title: The fate of hidden symmetries under magnetic Harrison transformations
papers.abstract: Solution-generating transformations construct new geometries from known seeds, raising the question of whether and to what extent the resulting solutions inherit the hidden symmetries underlying the seeds' integrability and separability. We have established universal perturbative inheritance laws for CKTs and massless scalar separability directly at the level of magnetic Harrison transformations, encompassing both magnetization of Carter-type seeds and demagnetization of conformal Carter-type seeds. In both magnetized Kerr and demagnetized Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson, this perturbative inheritance coexists with the loss of exact Carter-type separability, while seed-connected conformal Killing-Yano structures are already obstructed at the same perturbative order. These results reveal a hierarchy in the perturbative survival of hidden symmetries and provide a framework for investigating their inheritance in more general theoretical settings and under other solution-generating transformations.

papers.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models and Agentic Patterns for Static Code Analysis Warning Classification
papers.abstract: Context: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools support software verification and validation, reducing the time and cost of code reviews. However, the best SCA tools in the practitioner community generate a high volume of false positives, which developers tend to ignore, leading to genuine warnings being overlooked. Accordingly, studies increasingly adopt Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify and reduce false positives. Existing studies have produced promising results on public datasets, but underperformed on unseen datasets. Moreover, researchers do not leverage the full potential of Agentic patterns in LLMs or incorporate established code quality standards for warning classification. Objectives: This study utilises four manually annotated datasets to evaluate the performance of three contemporary LLMs for SCA warning classification in real-world applications, and incorporates Agentic patterns and established coding standards to enhance models' performance, addressing gaps identified in existing studies. Method: Three LLMs were selected using the LiveCodeBench benchmark, and the Structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) prompting technique was used to evaluate these LLMs. Furthermore, we incorporated Agentic patterns, such as Debating and Self-Consistency, to potentially improve performance in SCA warning classification. Results: Our results show that the performance of different LLMs varies with the characteristics of the dataset, ranging from 0.52 to 0.96 F1-Score for the best models. Additionally, the use of Agentic patterns does not improve LLMs' performance in most scenarios. Conclusions: SCA warning classification using LLMs works best only with certain warning types. We recommend evaluating LLMs in real-world applications rather than using publicly available datasets/benchmarks to understand their full utility.

papers.title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
