Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.

papers.title: SERAG: SEmantical and Relational approach for Anomaly detection on knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs constructed from text can contain facts that are individually plausible yet inconsistent with their relational context. We introduce SERAG, a supervised anomaly detector that combines two complementary plausibility estimates: a semantic score computed from separately encoded subject, relation, and object labels, and a relational score obtained through a relational graph convolutional network. The scores are standardized, calibrated, and fused. We evaluate the method on a subset of ICEWS18 with vocabulary-constrained synthetic anomalies generated by an LLM, using pooled and chronological splits. At 10% anomaly prevalence, SERAG achieves test AUPRCs of 0.321 and 0.258, respectively, compared with 0.159 and 0.146 for the strongest adapted baseline. Fusion improves mean test AUPRC over either branch alone, with a larger gain in the pooled protocol and a smaller validation-selected gain in the chronological protocol. Additional anomaly supervision improves performance. These results support the complementarity of textual and relational signals for detecting synthetic anomalies under the evaluated protocols.

papers.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
papers.abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

papers.title: GRAFT: Cross-Backbone LoRA Reuse for Continual Language and Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.

papers.title: ReVision: Selective Intrinsic Reasoning for Tool-Augmented, Reasoning-Intensive VQA
papers.abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

papers.title: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing: The operational value of continual machine learning
papers.abstract: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

papers.title: Multimodal Fusion with Pre-trained Models for Psychotherapy Outcome Prediction from Emotional Dynamics
papers.abstract: In-session emotional dynamics are associated with psychotherapy outcomes but difficult to measure at scale. Pretrained multimodal models provide automated access to facial, vocal, and textual signals, yet clinical datasets remain small. Our research question is how pretrained multimodal representations can best support psychotherapy outcome prediction under data scarcity. Three studies use 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine session-level outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS). Study 1 asks whether deep learning outperforms classical machine learning: a two-stage deep pipeline, first predicting window-level valence/arousal and then session outcomes, transferred poorly (best single configuration, $r=.078$). Study 2 asks which representation and preprocessing choices work best: statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models achieved average $r=.406$ across nine scales under per-scale configuration selection, up to $r=.490$ for symptom distress, with complementary modalities and no significant benefit from manual affect annotations or therapist features. Study 3 asks whether deep learning remains inferior under these choices: classical models outperformed an optimized single-stage deep model at the single-configuration level ($r=.281$ vs. $.222$) and on all nine scales under matched per-scale selection ($.406$ vs. $.252$). The results suggest that under clinical data scarcity, pretrained representations with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned aggregation.

papers.title: Brain AI Scientist: An Evidence-Based Multi-Agent System for Translational Neuroimaging in Precision Psychiatry
papers.abstract: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) has revealed widespread brain-network alterations in psychiatric disorders, yet translating these findings into individualized clinical decision support remains challenging. Here we introduce Brain AI Scientist, an autonomous multi-agent framework that integrates patient-specific fMRI, clinical information, and scientific evidence through retrieval, verification, and prioritization. Guided by Research Domain Criteria and evidence-based medicine, it builds traceable chains linking phenotypes, anatomical abnormalities, biomarkers, mechanisms, interventions, and validation strategies. In a representative autism case, Brain AI Scientist generated 37 anatomical hypotheses, retained 26 after literature verification, and derived 65 evidence-supported biomarkers from 90 unique publications to generate patient-specific treatment and validation guidance. Across 17 autism spectrum disorder cases, it outperformed GPT-3.5 baselines with and without fMRI impression in evidence grounding, personalization, clinical actionability, and biomarker-treatment reasoning. Brain AI Scientist therefore provides an auditable framework for translating patient-specific neuroimaging into individualized clinical decision support for precision psychiatry.

papers.title: Minimum cores in lattice graphs: zonotope structure and quartic growth
papers.abstract: A core of a graph is a nonempty vertex set in which every member has at least as many neighbours inside the set as outside. We study the minimum size $c_{m,n}$ of a finite core in the graph on $\Z^m$ joining points at sup-norm distance at most $n$. The local majority condition imposes a global geometric constraint: the convex hull of every core has an explicit lattice zonotope $H_n^{(m)}$ as a Minkowski summand. In the plane, this zonotope has width asymptotic to $6\zeta(3)n^3/\pi^2$. We prove that all its lattice points form a core and construct a shell with $O(n^4)$ points. Together with a packing argument, this gives $c_{2,n}=\Theta(n^4)$ and coordinate widths $\Theta(n^3)$ for every minimum core. We determine $c_{2,1}=12$ and $c_{2,2}=96$ by analytic arguments and prove uniqueness up to translation in both cases. Explicit forced-set and deficit certificates determine further minima within the prescribed zonotope hull. We distinguish these restricted results from global optimality and state the remaining geometric conjectures. We also give a direct reduction from \textsc{Clique} showing that the core problem is NP-complete on general finite graphs, which settles a conjecture of Hassanpour in the terms in which it was posed.

papers.title: LLMs in DevSecOps: A Systematic Mapping of Models, Evidence, and Research Gaps Across the Software Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into software security and DevSecOps workflows, yet their adoption, evaluation, and maturity vary substantially across lifecycle stages. This study systematically maps recent LLM-enabled security research published between 2024 and 2026 (until June) across six DevSecOps stages: \textit{Plan}, \textit{Code}, \textit{Test}, \textit{Review}, \textit{Deploy}, and \textit{Monitor}. For each stage, we analyze the security tasks addressed, models and adaptation strategies employed, evaluation settings, reported effectiveness, and key limitations. Our findings reveal an uneven research landscape, with \textit{Test} and \textit{Code} receiving substantially greater attention than \textit{Deploy} and \textit{Review}. Across stages, recent systems increasingly rely on structured context, iterative reasoning, fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, or agentic workflows rather than direct single-shot prompting. However, reported performance remains difficult to compare because studies use heterogeneous tasks, datasets, metrics, and baselines. Furthermore, most approaches are evaluated using benchmarks or open-source repositories, while industrial-scale evidence remains limited. We also find that existing systems are predominantly stage-specific, with little evidence of LLM-enabled security reasoning spanning multiple DevSecOps stages. Based on these observations, we identify research opportunities in standardized evaluation, production-scale validation, supply-chain and Infrastructure-as-Code security, trustworthy autonomous remediation, and cross-stage LLM integration. This study provides a recent lifecycle-level view of where LLM-enabled DevSecOps research is concentrated, what methodological patterns are emerging, and where significant gaps remain.

papers.title: Beyond Binary Audits: Does Guideline Grounding Mitigate Decision-Space Framing in LLM Opioid Prescribing?
papers.abstract: Audits of LLMs for bias in opioid prescribing have largely relied on binary treatment decisions, a signal that current models have saturated. We introduce Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test that holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and the granularity of the available dosage options. Adding an intermediate dosage option to otherwise unchanged vignettes substantially lowers agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences in dosage decisions remain small in all but one configuration once clinical risk factors are added. Grounding models in perioperative guidelines through retrieval reduces this framing effect on average but does not eliminate it, and one model's treatment decisions change when the retrieved passages are reordered. These results suggest that audits should vary the answer format, not only patient identity. We will release our codebase as well as Guideline-RAG-associated resources on GitHub ( this https URL ).

papers.title: All the Pieces Matter! A Six-stage Analysis of an Underground Fraud Ecosystem on Dread
papers.abstract: Cyber-enabled fraud is a dominant global threat that causes severe financial loss, identity theft, and widespread psychological harm. This illicit economy relies on a highly specialized underground ecosystem where distinct actors exchange technical tools, operational techniques, and laundering channels. This research presents a case study of one such live fraud ecosystem from the perspective of a cohesive six-stage value chain spanning from preparation to monetization: Capability, Data Acquisition, Technique Sharing, Identity Forgery, Execution, and Extraction. Analyzing 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments from nine communities on the Tor-based darknet forum Dread, we map user trajectories, content distribution, and the adoption of generative AI. Our findings show that structural cohesion within the ecosystem is maintained by a thin layer of `bridgers' who generate the majority of all content. Against a degree-preserving null model, three knowledge-building upstream stages of the value chain form a tightly coupled cluster, whereas the remaining three operational downstream stages resolve into highly specialized populations with small personnel overlap. Finally, we demonstrate that generative AI is being rapidly but unevenly absorbed across the value chain; the technology saturates knowledge-building communities while operational stages remain largely untouched. By quantifying criminal specialization and structural integration, our network-based approach provides a framework for targeted, high-impact law enforcement interventions.

papers.title: Decision 1.0: Towards Open Decision Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Intelligent software needs reusable judgments inside its control flow: selecting an action, testing a condition, or assessing evidence against a rubric. We present Decision 1.0, an open-weight family that turns textual state and runtime-defined questions into typed probability distributions. Its Choice, Noul, and Score interface lets applications specify outcomes at inference time and compose predictions into agents and workflows. Each question produces its candidate distribution without autoregressive text generation. Six models cover bidirectional encoder and causal decoder architectures, including a workflow specialist. Training draws on verifiable tasks, natural-language annotations, and workflow adaptation. On a common decision benchmark, Lux-9B achieves 84.17\% on explicit decisions and 91.25\% on inference, with a weighted overall score of 77.22\%. Results also expose gaps in composition, transfer, and probability calibration. Released weights and inference code provide a basis for developing decision models as reusable components of software.

papers.title: EmoTrace: Recursive Trace-Factorized Generation for Emotional Support Conversation
papers.abstract: Fundamental to effective emotional support is the iterative interpersonal dynamic wherein a supporter intervention continuously shapes the psychological trajectory of the seeker. While contemporary models capture variables at the turn level, including transient emotions and discrete strategies, they inherently treat these factors as isolated events. By retaining strictly literal dialogue histories while discarding the underlying decision logic, such architectures remain fundamentally incapable of sustaining coherent extended support. Here we introduce EmoTrace, a recursive method utilizing trace factorization to preserve explicit decision continuity throughout interactions spanning multiple turns. Departing from others, our approach formulates each conversational turn as a structured interaction increment encapsulating the evolving state of the seeker, the selected strategy, the affect of the supporter, and the ultimate textual realization. Accumulated sequentially, this trajectory of increments functions as an explicit structural trace informing subsequent interventions. Optimization of this factorized generation is achieved through two complementary mechanisms. Specifically, a value guidance mechanism aligns discrete factor selection with interaction values over an extended horizon, whereas a trace conditioning mechanism refines textual realization contingent upon the fixed strategic trace. Empirical evaluations across standard benchmarks demonstrate that EmoTrace yields substantial improvements in both strategic planning and response generation. Crucially, rollouts spanning multiple turns reveal that these retained structural traces confer compounding benefits over extended dialogues, establishing a robust mechanism for sustained affective alignment in human-machine interaction.

papers.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

papers.title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction
papers.abstract: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

papers.title: Ensemble Bounds for Pairwise Dissimilar Decomposition of Deterministic Datasets
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study reduced similarity decompositions of \emph{deterministic} datasets using redundancy graphs and obtain \emph{ensemble} bounds for the minimum size of such constrained decomposition. We consider batch decompositions that reduce similarity \emph{across} batches and use the Lovász local lemma to obtain bounds for the minimum size of a decomposition with a given pairwise dissimilarity. We then consider unique batch decomposition with a given relaxation parameter and obtain upper and lower ensemble bounds for the minimum size. Throughout, we use Binomial random graphs to obtain the desired ensemble bounds, by conditioning on the number of similar \emph{pairs} of data points.

papers.title: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents
papers.abstract: Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing this gap as \emph{Skill Transfer}: holding the skill's capability ceiling and the model's parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well. Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures, localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at this https URL

papers.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence
papers.abstract: Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically pair claims with clean, curated evidence in high-resource languages, but real-world evidence is often incomplete, misleading, or written in a language where models are weaker. We evaluate the robustness of fact-checking LLMs for different languages. Building on EuroVerdict, we construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of English, German, Greek, and Romanian, then apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels. We test LLMs on a set of claims, providing them with evidence from the sets above. A rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge scores reasoning quality. Verdict accuracy proves highly sensitive to both factors: Misleading edit cut Llama 3.1 8B's English accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, and losses widen as language resource level decreases. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers much, but not all, of the low-resource gap. Judge scores decline more slowly than accuracy, suggesting that automated reasoning evaluation underestimates degradation. These results caution against deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence, and we release our evidence datasets and evaluation code to support future work.

papers.title: RGFC: Registry Grounded Function Calling with stage-decomposed evaluation
papers.abstract: Tool-calling evaluations often report whether the final call matches a reference answer, but this single outcome merges different failures: choosing a function outside the available registry, violating the selected schema, or filling arguments with values not supported by the user request. These failures matter more when models must choose from larger tool registries. We introduce RFCD, a registry-scaled function-calling benchmark built from BFCL, Glaive Function Calling v2, and Tool-Call-Data, with standardized JSON-schema registries ranging from 5 to 3,000 functions. We also introduce TAAG, a deterministic stage-decomposed evaluator for registry conformance, structural completeness, and argument grounding. Across six locally served sub-4B models, three data sources, and four feedback modes, registry scale is the dominant source of degradation: single-pass TAAG pass rate drops sharply from small to large registries on all sources. Repeated feedback improves some grounding metrics but adds substantial token cost and does not consistently improve end-to-end F1. Requirement-level TAAG-R feedback gives modest gains over stage-only TAAG-S feedback, which indicates that TAAG signals are useful for analysis and correction probes but do not solve registry scaling by themselves. RFCD and TAAG provide an evaluation resource for measuring where tool-calling systems fail as registries grow.

papers.title: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study
papers.abstract: Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed. These findings suggest that target-aligned conjecture generation depends on combining information that identifies relevant objects with information that constrains admissible claims.

papers.title: CondRelBench: A Mixed-Domain Benchmark for Condition-Scoped Relation Understanding
papers.abstract: Relation extraction systems often identify what a relation is, but not the condition under which it holds. This can collapse condition-bound claims into unsupported generalizations, a failure we call relation overgeneralization. We introduce CondRelBench, a mixed-domain benchmark for evaluating condition-scoped relation understanding. Each claim is represented as (E1, R, E2 | C), where C is the condition licensing the relation. Using 3,000 synthetic paragraphs, 200 PubMed full-text papers, and 695 Reddit posts, we construct five probe variants per tuple that preserve, replace, remove, or contradict the condition, or contradict the relation itself. Models classify each probe as Supported, Not Supported, or Not Enough Evidence. We also introduce Overgeneralization Rate (OGR) and Scope Preservation Score (SPS) to measure false support for altered claims and consistency across probe families. Across prompted LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models, we find that Accuracy and Macro F1 often hide scope failures. Models frequently support the original scoped claim but fail when its condition is removed or altered. Domain-specific encoders achieve the strongest scope preservation, while instruction-tuned LLMs often show higher overgeneralization. Synthetic supervision helps but does not close the gap to real-world PubMed and Reddit performance.

papers.title: Assisting Patients with Reliable Information Gathering: A Guide to Building Efficient QA Systems for Medical Use
papers.abstract: The application of question-answering (QA) systems in the medical domain has rapidly advanced, significantly improving patients' access to reliable health-related information. However, current approaches face notable challenges, including the difficulty in obtaining large-scale and unbiased medical datasets, significant privacy concerns, and inefficiencies due to manual dataset annotation. To address these issues, This study introduce a novel methodology leveraging publicly accessible online health forums to systematically build an unbiased, privacy-conscious QA dataset, and it employs Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) for automated topic identification, enabling efficient and targeted annotation of relevant patient-generated content. Subsequently, this study propose a two-stage QA pipeline based on a Retriever-Reader architecture, which is further enhanced through fine-tuning state-of-the-art transformer-based models on the constructed domain-specific QA dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our fine-tuned BioBERT significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, offering accurate patient-derived insights and providing a replicable framework for building efficient medical QA systems.

papers.title: All edges lead to Rome: analyzing Late Antiquity regime shifts using coin hoard data
papers.abstract: Complex network analysis and other statistical techniques can be fruitfully applied to historical data to understand dynamics that brought the territory under study to a certain state. In this paper we use the FLAME database to understand when a drastic change of trade regime occurred in the Italian peninsula by looking at mint-hoard links that are evidence of a physical connection between them. By using changepoint analysis to pinpoint precise dates in the time series of these links, and then historical as well as network data to establish the sequence of network collapse, we find that the demise of the Western Roman Empire started at the beginning of the 5th century AD, yielding a more precise sequence of how and when it reached Italia.

papers.title: Intrinsic Attention as Navigator: A Non-Generative Retrieval Method for Multi-Hop Queries
papers.abstract: For multi-hop queries in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), it is crucial to accurately obtain evidence pieces. In this study, we propose a training-free method for multi-hop query retrieval, named Intrinsic Navigating-based Non-Generative Retrieval (IN-Retriever). Instead of generating intermediate reasoning text, the method extracts the bridging clue from the internal attention of the embedding model based on the current context and retrieved candidate documents. During iterative clue extraction and document retrieval, IN-Retriever strips away revealed clues from the embedded query vector and then reranks candidate documents in a targeted manner, thereby steering retrieval toward hidden next-hop evidence. In the experiments, we confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of using intrinsic attention signals to guide external multi-hop retrieval. Experimental results show that our method precisely collects sufficient documents to support multi-hop queries and significantly outperforms sparse and dense retrieval methods.

papers.title: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate model-generated medical content, creating a potential circularity: an LLM judge may favor outputs generated by the same model independently of clinical quality. To characterize LLM judge self-preference in medical settings, we measured same-model affinity in single-turn specialist question answering and multi-turn standardized-patient encounters. We evaluated eight models, two from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen, on 620 real point of care questions from clinicians (Real-POCQi). The same eight models also generated and judged 200 standardized patient-clinician scenarios (MedSP1000) up to 8 visible turns. In total, our analysis spans 13,760 LLM judgments. We define three complementary measures of self-preference. Answer Rank Bias, our primary measure, compared the rank assigned to a fixed response by its own-model judge with its average rank from outside judges. Answer Score Bias made the analogous comparison using rubric scores. Own-Answer Win Rate measured how often a judge ranked its own model's response above a competitor. Higher values across all these measures indicate greater degrees of self-preference. In Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias was $+1.22$ positions, and all eight judges favored their own answers. Self-preference persisted both with and without a grading rubric. Revealing generator identities modestly weakened self-preference by an average of $-0.094$ positions. In MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranged from $+0.53$ to $+0.62$ positions, with no clear difference by conversation length ($p=0.17$). LLM judges systematically favored responses generated by their own models across multiple formats. Clinical AI deployments should exercise increased vigilance including multiple evaluation measures and judge panels spanning differing model families when deploying LLM-as-a-judge systems.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
papers.abstract: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and cutting DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.

papers.title: Physics-informed and event-aware forecasting of ammonia emissions in aerobic chicken manure composting bioreactors: A PINN-PatchTST-GPR framework with symbolic dynamic extraction
papers.abstract: Predicting ammonia (NH3) concentrations during aerobic chicken manure composting provides critical feedforward signals for intelligent aeration. However, the concurrence of long-term biochemical evolution and intermittent forced-aeration pulses poses significant modeling hurdles across steady baselines, transient surges, and risk quantification. Existing data-driven models lack physical consistency, while mechanistic kinetic models struggle with environmental disturbances. To bridge this gap, we propose PINN-PatchTST-GPR, a physics-informed neuro-symbolic forecasting framework. Validated on a 28-day composting campaign across six vertical bioreactors, the framework couples a channel-independent PatchTST backbone with macroscopic kinetic constraints, dynamic physical bounds, and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist. Multi-channel sensor streams drive discrete differential equation residuals and non-negativity bounds, strictly ensuring physical plausibility. A block-split conformal prediction module yields nominal 90% distribution-free prediction intervals, while PySINDy and PySR extract low-complexity symbolic equations for quiescent and surge regimes. The model achieves an overall RMSE of 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and Etime of 0.7 +/- 0.2 min. For uncertainty quantification, it attains PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%, MPIW of 6.951 +/- 0.128 ppm, and IS0.1 of 6.968 +/- 0.128 ppm. Symbolically, PySINDy yields an RMSE of 0.4624 +/- 0.0758 ppm (R2 = 0.9896), while PySR yields 2.4084 +/- 0.0864 ppm (R2 = 0.9523). Biologically, the 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions. Overall, PINN-PatchTST-GPR harmonizes global forecasting, localized transient responsiveness, and risk quantification for precision composting.

papers.title: Bridging Semantics and Utilities: A Controllable and Scalable Market Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models(LLMs) have recently been used to construct generative agents for financial market simulation. Existing approaches typically prompt each agent separately with public market information and a private investor profile, and ask the model to directly generate trading actions. In this agent-wise design, the model repeatedly interprets information shared across the population, while individual behavior is controlled through textual descriptions of investor preferences and traits. This creates two structural difficulties: continuous traits such as risk sensitivity do not reliably induce ordered behavioral changes, and repeatedly processing the same public information causes inference costs to grow with the number of agents. We propose \textbf{SUM}, a Semantic-Utility Model that separates cohort-level semantic perception from agent-level utility-based decision-making. A language model interprets public market information for each investor type and produces semantic signals shared within the corresponding cohort. Individual agents then combine these signals with their private states, preferences, and constraints to generate orders through utility-based decisions. Experiments in an A-share limit-order-book market show that \textbf{SUM} provides more stable and monotonic behavioral control than prompt-based agents while substantially reducing repeated language-model inference as the population grows. Closed-loop simulations further reproduce directional market responses, volatility persistence, differentiated investment styles, and persistent wealth heterogeneity. These results establish \textbf{SUM} as a controllable, scalable, and semantically informed framework for financial market simulation.

papers.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
papers.abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

papers.title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

papers.title: NYUAD at ImageEval Shared Tasks: A Multimodal LLM for Audio-Visual Question Answering and Hallucination Detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled more natural interaction with visual and spoken information, creating new opportunities for intelligent audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection systems. AVQA extends traditional visual question answering by requiring models to jointly understand an input image and a spoken question to generate accurate, context-aware responses. Despite recent advances, AVQA and hallucination detection tasks remain challenging for modern standard Arabic (MSA) due to the limited availability of multimodal datasets and the need to reason across Arabic speech and text modalities alongside visual inputs. In this paper, we present an MLLM-based framework for AVQA that takes an image and a spoken question as input and generates answers. In addition, we utilized this framework to detect hallucination in text-image pairs. The proposed approach is evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Task (Ayn-VQA) benchmark, which focuses on culturally grounded Arabic AVQA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively understands spoken queries, grounds their responses in the visual content, and produces accurate answers. The results underscore the capacity and limitations of different LLM architectures for both English and MSA and under various conditions.

papers.title: Many Paths to the Same Mistake: Generating Diverse Reasoning Paths Behind the Same Student Mistake
papers.abstract: Realistic evaluation of AI systems requires user simulators that capture not only cooperative behavior, but also the errors and variability that arise in real interactions. In educational technology, simulating step-by-step flawed student reasoning is essential, yet datasets mapping these pathways are scarce, and Large Language Models (LLMs) often auto-correct rather than sustain simulated mistakes. To address this, we present a generate-and-filter pipeline that produces diverse and realistic student error traces. Our approach utilizes forward consistency, a metric verifying if a flawed reasoning trace can be used to recover the student's actual incorrect answer, paired with an LLM-as-a-judge to ensure realism. Our evaluation suggests that while many LLMs struggle to maintain incorrect reasoning mid-trace, smaller supervised fine-tuned models successfully capture these divergent paths. This work provides a framework for high-fidelity error trace generation, advancing realistic, non-cooperative user simulation.

papers.title: NYUAD at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Embedding Models for Detecting Arabic Hateful Memes and Unsafe Prompts
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of social media and generative AI has significantly increased the volume of Arabic textual content, memes, and user prompts shared across online platforms. While these media facilitate communication, creativity, and information exchange, they can also be exploited to disseminate hate speech, harmful content, and unsafe instructions. As a result, there is an increasing need for reliable automated methods to identify hateful Arabic memes and harmful (unsafe) prompts. This paper leverages pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to learn rich semantic representations from textual and visual content. The evaluation is conducted using a dataset of Arabic memes and prompts proposed in the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 challenge. The results underscore the capacity of large language model (LLM)-based embedding models to deliver superior performance. Developing robust detection systems is essential for improving content moderation and fostering a more secure and trustworthy online environment for Arabic-speaking users.

papers.title: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
papers.abstract: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

papers.title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
papers.abstract: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

papers.title: Enhanced English-Sanskrit Translation using Multilingual NMT Approach
papers.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is a widely accepted technique of automatic translation tasks of Natural Language Processing. However, NMT requires a sufficient amount of parallel corpora to attain a reasonable translation quality. In this work, we have considered a low-resource English-Sanskrit pair for English-to-Sanskrit and Sanskrit-to-English translation. We have performed a comparative analysis by exploring bilingual and multilingual approaches using LSTM-based Sequence-to-Sequence, and fine-tuning a pretrained model IndicTrans in a multilingual NMT approach. To investigate multilingual transfer learning, we additionally construct multilingual translation settings by incorporating Hindi along with English and Sanskrit using language-tagged data. Experimental results demonstrate that IndicTrans-based multilingual models outperform baseline results in terms of automatic evaluation metrics such as BLEU and ChrF for both directions of translation.

papers.title: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Online caregiver forums are an important source of emotional and informational support for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). We compare responses to 85 real caregiver questions from ALZConnected across four responder groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and a retrieval-augmented CareGPT grounded in peer discussions. Using 28 measures spanning linguistic form, emotional support, informational support, and topic scope, we examine how these voices differ when answering the same questions. Peers provided time-anchored narratives and community grounding; clinicians offered concise, advice-forward, clinically bounded guidance; and LLMs produced a formal, verbose, highly structured consultation style. CareGPT showed minimal measurable separation from ChatGPT, suggesting that retrieval plus prompt injection alone was insufficient to shift communicative stance. LLM outputs scored higher than peers on politeness and emotion-support markers and were comparable to clinicians on informativeness and physician-alignment measures, but were less narrative and less contextually situated. Topic modeling showed that LLM responses concentrated on advice-oriented themes, whereas peers covered a broader range, including emotional processing, legal and financial concerns, and daily care. These findings suggest that AI can complement, but not replace, human contributions to ADRD caregiver support and motivate hybrid systems that combine structured AI delivery with the distinct strengths of human voices.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Decision Support in Gait Analysis: A Proof-of-Concept
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential for clinical decision support but lack specialized biomechanical knowledge required for accurate gait analysis interpretation. We developed and evaluated a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to enhance LLM-generated clinical explanations for ankle fracture rehabilitation using ground reaction force data. Using the GaitRec dataset (503 subjects: 211 healthy, 292 ankle fracture patients), we implemented a five-stage pipeline integrating: (1) machine learning classification (91.3\% accuracy); (2) Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for explainable feature identification; (3) RAG knowledge base from peer-reviewed biomechanics literature; (4) GPT-5 explanation generation with and without retrieval augmentation; and (5) double-blind evaluation by experienced physical therapists across five clinical criteria. RAG augmentation produced statistically significant improvements in Clini-cal Benefit (mean difference=0.60, p=0.047, {\delta}=0.49) and Completeness (mean difference=0.70, p=0.049, {\delta}=0.49), both demonstrating large effect sizes. Baseline GPT-5 achieved strong performance across all criteria (\textgreater4.0/5.0). This proof-of-concept demonstrates that augmenting general-purpose LLMs with domain-specific knowledge meaningfully enhances actionable, evidence-based clinical guidance---dimensions most critical for rehabilitation decision-making. The framework provides a scalable approach for integrating AI into specialized clinical workflows without costly model retraining.

papers.title: Internal Verdicts Track Evidence: A Template-Controlled Neutrosophic Reading of Epistemic States in Large Language Models via the Jacobian Lens
papers.abstract: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.

papers.title: Jailbreak LLMs with Linguistic Style as a Hidden Attack Surface
papers.abstract: We show that linguistic style is a systematic and previously overlooked attack surface for LLM safety. Across a diverse taxonomy of styles and multiple state-of-the-art models, stylistic rewrites of identical harmful goals produce order-of-magnitude differences in Attack Success Rate (ASR), with some styles achieving up to 80\% ASR while others remain below 6\%. To exploit this vulnerability, we introduce a lightweight single-pass attack framework that combines a style-conditioned generator with a BERT-based style selector, achieving performance competitive with substantially more expensive multi-turn optimization methods. To understand why style affects safety behavior, we conduct mechanistic analysis on LLaMA-3.1-8B and find that stylistic rewrites disrupt refusal representations while preserving recoverable harmful intent, suggesting a distributed failure mode rather than a single refusal mechanism. Motivated by this finding, we develop a style-aware Direct Preference Optimization defense that reduces ASR from 86\% to 19.5\% while largely preserving utility. Together, our results establish linguistic style as a critical factor in adversarial robustness and provide both mechanistic insight and a practical defense.

papers.title: ScopeBench: Evaluating Cultural Norm Scope Awareness in LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety evaluation in large language models treats harm as culturally invariant, yet a model cannot correctly apply a safety norm without knowing whose norms bind. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark that treats cultural scope as a first-class safety dimension. It comprises 3,323 norms spanning 49 countries across nine cultural clusters, each annotated as Universal or Specific. We define three scope error types identically across four evaluation tasks: Scope Inflation, Scope Deflation, and Scope Displacement. Evaluating 21 frontier LLMs across seven model families, we surface three structural failures. First, the dominant error type inverts with prompt format: Scope Deflation reaches 70% in single-answer classification, while Scope Inflation reaches 33% when each candidate culture is judged independently. Second, scope-classification accuracy is empirically decoupled from behavioral safety: the six classifiers achieving at least 97% Task 1 accuracy still produce harmful responses to 40-42% of scope-violating statements. Third, no model is safe in interaction, with harmful-response rates ranging from 29% to 51% across the cohort, excluding one model that systematically refuses the task. We release all data, code, and model outputs to establish cultural scope as a distinct alignment axis.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Mambas Selective Gate in Financial Markets: A Leakage-Controlled Study
papers.abstract: Selectively gated state-space models (SSMs), notably Mamba, are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes (bull, bear, sideways) remains opaque. This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) to a six-layer Mamba trained on approximately twenty-one years of daily data for a point-in-time set of S&P 500 constituents plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decomposing per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our central contribution is methodological and cautionary. A prior, uncontrolled configuration recovered market regimes from SAE features at F1 = 1.00. Under a controlled protocol that (i) removes the three input features that overlap the HMM label definition, (ii) disables the auxiliary regime-classification head, (iii) uses a point-in-time constituent universe, and (iv) evaluates against labels disjoint from the inputs, the same regime label is recovered at only F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and from an SAE trained on a randomly initialized, untrained Mamba (0.364). A 2x2 attribution grid shows the near-perfect result is an interaction of auxiliary supervision and label-defining inputs: neither factor alone exceeds F1 ~ 0.40. Effect sizes with block-bootstrap inference show the residual selective-gate (Delta t) regime effect is statistically detectable but economically negligible and uniform across layers rather than layer-specialized; the apparent polysemanticity gradient disappears under continuous, theory-grounded measures. We contribute a reproducible leakage-control protocol for interpretability evaluation of financial SSMs, a quantified demonstration that previously reported regime structure is a label-contamination artifact, and a modest economically grounded feature subset that genuinely survives the controls.

papers.title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification
papers.abstract: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences. We present a controlled empirical benchmark that measures the inflation in held-out ROC-AUC caused by five common leakage mechanisms: global standardization, global median imputation, duplicate contamination, supervised feature selection before splitting, and target encoding before splitting. The benchmark spans six public datasets and two synthetic stress tests, three model families, and five repeated stratified train/test splits, yielding 600 paired clean-versus-leaked comparisons. To avoid pseudo-replication, inference is performed on dataset-level effects with cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Label-dependent or direct data-reuse mechanisms produced systematic optimism: global target encoding increased ROC-AUC by 2.42 percentage points on average (95% cluster-bootstrap CI 0.62--4.89), global supervised feature selection by 1.93 points (0.63--3.39), and duplicate contamination by 1.52 points (0.40--2.80). All three remained significant after multiplicity correction. In contrast, global scaling and global median imputation had near-zero average effects under the i.i.d. settings studied here. A controlled target-encoding stress test further shows that leakage becomes sharply worse as categories become sparse. The results support a severity-aware view of leakage: evaluation pipelines should prevent all held-out-data dependence, but label-dependent transformations and observation reuse deserve especially aggressive auditing.

papers.title: Skill-Latent Rewards: LLM-Guided Reward Formulation for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.

papers.title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

papers.title: Profiling Hallucinations in Frontier LLMs for Entity Linking to Medical Ontologies
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into healthcare promises to revolutionize clinical documentation and interoperability, yet reliability remains a concern. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of hallucinations by frontier LLMs tasked with mapping clinical text to SNOMED CT. Through rigorous experimentation, we identify a critical reliability gap: LLMs hallucinate medical codes at a rate that currently renders them unsuitable for autonomous clinical coding applications. Paradoxically, constraining models to use ground-truth mention spans exacerbates, rather than mitigates, these hallucinations. We further contribute a taxonomy of hallucination types--including deprecated codes and cross-ontology errors--and demonstrate that general-purpose LLMs significantly underperform compared to specialized zero-shot entity linking approaches. These findings underscore the need for robust verification mechanisms before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Whose Side Are You On? Measuring Stance at Scale for Reddit Discourse Analysis During the Israel-Gaza War
papers.abstract: Large-scale discourse analysis often requires stance labels, yet for many high-salience political events such labels are unavailable at the comment level. We introduce and validate a comment-level stance measurement instrument that assigns Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestinian, or Undefined stance using Reddit comment text. The instrument is calibrated from a small, manually annotated gold-standard dataset and scaled through large language model-assisted labeling, achieving weighted-$F_{1}=0.88$ against held-out human annotations. To enable corpus-scale measurement, we operationalize the instrument as a lightweight classifier based on DistilBERT embeddings and an RBF SVM, which achieves weighted-$F_{1}=0.7935$ on the original gold-standard set. Applying this instrument, we measure the stance of approximately 2.7 million Reddit comments posted between 2023 and 2025 during the Israel-Gaza war. We demonstrate what this measurement enables by analyzing stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations. This work shows how validated, low-cost stance measurement can support large-scale descriptive analysis of polarized discourse, without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.

papers.title: Theoretical Foundations of Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh)
papers.abstract: This paper presents the theoretical foundations and a comprehensive formal system for Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh). We begin by establishing six foundational principles that distinguish computational Fiqh from conventional natural language processing and general theological formalization. These principles define Islamic jurisprudence as a normative deductive science operating on empirically grounded facts, necessitating a dual inductive-deductive methodology, and requiring a logical foundation specifically engineered for Fiqh rather than adopted from existing formalisms. Based on these principles, we construct a three-layer stratified computational language, $\mathcal{F} = D \circ A \circ G$, consisting of: (1) an Arabic Morphological/Grammatical Grounding Engine that transforms fully vocalized Classical Arabic into language-independent Grounded Action Structures (GAS); (2) the Arabic Reified Action Calculus (ARAC) that normalizes these structures into canonical logical representations; and (3) a function-free Horn-clause Datalog engine for executable legal deduction. Furthermore, we introduce a bridging methodology (Algorithm $\Omega$) that dynamically generates a Fiqh-Categorized Attribute Grammar from inductively extracted Horn clauses via an Ontological Meta-Map ($\mathcal{M}_{onto}$), seamlessly connecting the inductive extraction of legal rules to their deductive application. The paper rigorously proves the system's semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, and decidability. Crucially, by leveraging morphosyntactic inflection markers ($\delta$ modes) as structural constraints, we prove the strict unambiguity of the proposed grammar, achieving deterministic $O(n)$ linear parsing complexity. This work provides a mathematically verifiable, epistemologically grounded, and computationally tractable foundation for automated Islamic jurisprudence.

papers.title: Endogenous Preferences as Vulnerability Signals: Discovering Universal Adversarial Triggers for LLM Utility Degradation
papers.abstract: Deployed large language models must remain useful when untrusted text enters their prompt context. Adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods typically define the failures they seek through task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. We ask whether a frozen model's clean behavior can reveal a reusable context vulnerability when its task-level form is unknown, and downstream task feedback is withheld. To study this question, EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design that compares the same frozen victim on clean and span-modified versions of each unlabeled instruction. Without a task-level target, the clean pass supplies the victim's preferred response-onset token as an instruction-conditioned reference; Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how insertion weakens that preference. An auxiliary generator supplies bounded-span proposals; EPD guides its update and ranks the pool without access to downstream information. The highest-scoring victim-specific span is fixed before evaluation and reused unchanged across all held-out inputs. Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater average degradation than every evaluated baseline under the reported protocols. Matched protocol ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection followed by fixed reuse than for null-context fixed reuse or per-input generation. Transfer recurs across proposers with proposal-dependent strength; output-level analyses identify victim-specific associations between trigger families and downstream failure patterns. Thus, clean behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs yet manifest through structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation. The code and data will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: Where Language Models Fail Like Aphasic Patients and Where They Don't
papers.abstract: The computational architecture of human word production -- whether semantic-lexical retrieval and phonological encoding constitute dissociable processing stages -- has been debated for decades using hand-designed models with small vocabularies. We introduce computational architectural dissociation: using known architectural properties of vision-language models (VLMs) to derive falsifiable predictions about which patient error types should and should not align with model errors under perturbation. Because VLMs perform picture naming through learned semantic competition over full vocabularies but lack phonological encoding entirely, perturbation-induced errors should match patient patterns for semantic-stage categories but not phonological ones. Testing LLaVA 1.6 (Vicuna-13B) against 88 patients with aphasia across 175 Philadelphia Naming Test items (~37 million naming attempts, 50 perturbation seeds), we find that six of eight error categories show significant item-level alignment (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.32-0.50, all p < 0.001) while the two phonological categories -- formal errors and abstruse neologisms -- show no alignment ($\rho$ = 0.110 and 0.084, both n.s.), confirming the predicted dissociation. Spectral analysis of the output probabilities places each error type at a distinct position in a six-dimensional space, giving a mechanistic interpretability tool. The dissociation is layer-specific (peaking at L22, 55% depth), severity-independent, and stable across seeds (split-half r > 0.998). Weight perturbation of four additional 7B VLMs spanning the tested architectural combinations produced correct-rate alignment of comparable magnitude ($\rho$ = 0.21-0.27). Whether the per-category dissociation itself depends on scale or on attention design requires a comparison within a single inference implementation, which is reported separately.

papers.title: Ethics Integration in CS Theory Courses
papers.abstract: The integration of ethics into computing curricula has gained substantial momentum, based on foundational work by the Embedded EthiCS movement, ACM/IEEE curricular recommendations, and a growing literature on ethics modules in courses on artificial intelligence, software engineering, human-computer interaction, and data science. One foundational area of the undergraduate computing curriculum remains absent from these efforts: CS theory. Courses on automata, computability, and complexity are widely perceived as too abstract or value-neutral for sustained ethical engagement, and the published record on ethics integration largely reflects this perception. In this position paper, we argue that theory courses are not merely compatible with ethics integration but offer a distinctive and underutilized perspective that complements theory itself. We synthesize the embedded-ethics literature, examine the standard objections to ethics in theory, and identify five avenues through which canonical theory results connect directly to substantive ethical questions: undecidability and the limits of automated reasoning, complexity-theoretic privacy and fairness, formal languages and pattern matching, the rhetoric of problem reductions, and randomization as an ethical primitive. We propose lightweight integration strategies grounded in existing pedagogical literature and respond to the most common instructor objections.

papers.title: OmniTag-LLM: Multilingual Multitask Speech Tagging
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs promise to replace the traditional cascade of specialist speech models with a single system that, from one audio clip, jointly transcribes and labels emotion, gender, language, and named entities. Yet most benchmarks still score these tasks in isolation, and largely in English. We introduce OmniTag-Bench, a five-language benchmark (en/de/es/fr/it) and training recipe for joint understanding: one audio clip in, one JSON object out (transcript, emotion, gender, LID, token-level NER). We evaluate ten open multimodal LLMs and a LoRA fine-tuned Qwen3-Omni on a unified prompt and scorer. Beyond aggregate scores, OmniTag-Bench reveals a systematic failure mode: several strong models often transcribe or translate non-English speech into English, inflating multilingual WER. Fine-tuning improves the base model on NER, emotion, and WER while nearly doubling accuracy on independent human-labeled emotion corpora, suggesting transferable gains beyond pseudo-label imitation. The fine-tuned model also generalizes to unseen but related languages, transferring to held-out Dutch. We release prompts, the scorer, and the labeling pipeline.

papers.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
papers.abstract: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.

papers.title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
papers.abstract: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100.
